questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with recurrent pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea, and vomiting is diagnosed with biliary dyskinesia. Which of the following is least useful in the diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. USG

USG is the least useful investigation in the diagnosis of biliary dyskinesia or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction since the findings can be normal or show non-specific changes such as dilatation of the common bile duct.

Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) is caused due to a structurally or physiologically abnormal sphincter with a higher tone, which fails to relax, causing pain and recurrent episodes of pancreatitis with normal liver function tests. There are two clinical types: biliary SOD and pancreatic SOD. Each type is further classified into types 1,2 and 3.

Other options:

Option A: The best investigation for the diagnosis of SOD is ERCP with manometry of the biliary and pancreatic sphincters.

Option B: HIDA scan will show a reduced gallbladder ejection fraction (EF). A gallbladder EF <35% is considered diagnostic of biliary dyskinesia.

Option D: Biliary-type SOD should be considered and excluded in post-cholecystectomy syndrome; hence, post-surgery follow-up is essential.

CT and MRCP can demonstrate dilatation of the biliary and pancreatic ducts.
questions.learning: USG USG is the least useful investigation in the diagnosis of biliary dyskinesia or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction since the findings can be normal or show non-specific changes such as dilatation of the common bile duct.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with persistent fever and prolonged respiratory distress despite adequate treatment, with a past history of exposure to tuberculosis. Which combination of diagnostic findings is most likely in this case?
options: Positive skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
questions.explanation: Cryptic tuberculosis is a form of TB where classical diagnostic findings are absent, making it difficult to detect. It is often seen in elderly or immuno compromised patients. In such cases: 1. The tuberculin skin test (TST) may be negative due to anergy (poor immune response) 2. The chest X-ray may also appear normal or non-specific, lacking typical TB features like cavitation or infiltrates Despite this, the patient may still have systemic symptoms like fever and respiratory distress, which raises suspicion. Why Other Options Are Ruled Out (A) Positive TST + normal X-ray → suggests latent TB (B) Positive TST + positive X-ray → typical active TB, not cryptic (D) Negative TST + positive X-ray → suggests pathology but not “cryptic” presentation
questions.learning: Cryptic tuberculosis is a form of TB where classical diagnostic findings are absent, making it difficult to detect. It is often seen in elderly or immuno compromised patients.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old individual was involved in a motorcycle accident and presents with the following clinical or imaging findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical photograph shows the affected limb in a position of abduction and external rotation, which is pathognomonic for an anterior hip dislocation. This injury typically occurs during high-energy trauma, such as a bike accident, when a force is applied to an abducted leg. In contrast, posterior hip dislocation (Option B) is much more common (dashboard injury) and presents with the opposite deformity: flexion, adduction, and internal rotation. Superior hip dislocation (Option C) is extremely rare and usually associated with extensive pelvic fractures. Option D is incorrect as the clinical presentation for anterior and posterior dislocations is mutually exclusive due to the different positions of the femoral head. Therefore, the visible external rotation and abduction in this patient definitively identify the dislocation as anterior
questions.learning: The clinical photograph shows the affected limb in a position of abduction and external rotation, which is pathognomonic for an anterior hip dislocation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In children with GBS, all are true except?
options: Areflexia of the affected limb is a mandatory diagnostic criteria
Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
Intravenous immunoglobulin is the first line of management
Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases

Plasmapheresis is preferred in refractory cases of GBS.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy characterized by weakness, areflexia, and sensory symptoms. It often follows an infection, vaccination, or other immune trigger. The autoimmune mechanism attacks the peripheral nervous system, leading to demyelination or axonal damage.

Mandatory diagnostic criteria for GBS:

• Progressive, symmetric muscle weakness of more than one limb: Weakness evolves over a period of hours to weeks. Typically starts in the legs and ascends (ascending paralysis).

• Areflexia or hyporeflexia: Deep tendon reflexes are reduced or absent in affected limbs. Reflex loss is a hallmark clinical feature.

Symptoms:

• Progressive weakness, starting in the legs and moving upwards (ascending paralysis).
• Areflexia (loss of reflexes) or hyporeflexia in the affected limbs. (Option A)
• Sensory symptoms like tingling or numbness may occur but are less prominent.
• Autonomic dysfunction, such as fluctuations in heart rate or blood pressure, in severe cases.

CSF Findings:

• Albuminocytological dissociation: High protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with normal or low white blood cell counts. (Option D)

Treatment:

• Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): First-line therapy. (Option C)
• Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange): in severe or refractory cases. (Option B)
• Supportive care for respiratory or autonomic complications.
questions.learning: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases Plasmapheresis is preferred in refractory cases of GBS. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy characterized by weakness, areflexia, and sensory symptoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the following conditions? G6PD deficiency- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

Elective splenectomy is done in case of hereditary spherocytosis.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations of the red blood cell surface proteins spectrin and ankyrin can result in unstable cell membranes, leading to hemolysis.

This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice and fatigue. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones.

Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor. The diagnosis can be confirmed by the acid glycerol lysis test and the eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA)–binding test.

There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy. However, due to the possible adverse effects, it is only indicated in severe cases and after the child attains puberty in moderate cases. It should be followed up with the appropriate antibiotic and vaccine prophylaxis.

Other options:

Option (A): Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a type of inherited hemolytic anemia. It is associated with exacerbations after consuming anti-malarial drugs and in periods of oxidative stress. The peripheral smear shows characteristic "bite cells". In G6PD deficiency, uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is largely preventable by avoiding exposure to triggering factors.

Option (B): Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a hemolytic disorder that also presents with pancytopenia and a tendency to form venous thrombi. It occurs due to defective GPI anchors on the red blood cell surface which are normally used to anchor CD 59 (cell-protective proteins) to the surface. These patients can present with episodes of dark brown urine in the morning, anemia, pancytopenia, and recurrent abdominal pain due to thrombosis of abdominal veins.

Bone marrow transplantation is done for the treatment. Recently humanized monoclonal antibody eculizumab is used.

Option (D): Hairy cell leukemia is a distinctive B cell neoplasm, that predominantly affects middle-aged males. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is the cytochemical stain characteristically shown by leukemic hairy cells. Patients commonly present with massive splenomegaly due to infiltration of the leukemic cells. Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement can also be seen. These tumors respond well to chemotherapy and BRAF (B-type Raf proto-oncogene) inhibitors, and they have an excellent prognosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhalational agent of choice in a 10-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sevoflurane

Induction agent of choice in pediatric anesthesia is sevoflurane.

Although both halothane and sevoflurane provide a smooth induction, sevoflurane appears to have a greater therapeutic index than halothane and is the preferred agent for inhaled induction in pediatric anesthesia.

Isoflurane and desflurane are airway irritants. Hence not used for induction of anesthesia as they can precipitate laryngospasm. These agents are used only during maintenance of anesthesia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 47-year-old man presented with a chronic non-healing painless ulcer over his scalp for 8 years. He gave a history of sustaining electric burns injury to the scalp 8 years back. The examination findings are shown below. Which of the following statements is true?
options: It can progress to squamous cell cancer
Long duration antibiotics will improve the condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can progress to squamous cell cancer

The given scenario and image show a long-standing ulcer with crusting and irregular borders can progress to Marjolin's ulcer which is an aggressive type of squamous cell carcinoma.

Marjolin ulcers most commonly arise from burn scars. The most common cell type identified is squamous cell carcinoma. All suspicious lesions should be biopsied. Confirmed cases of Marjolin ulcers should be excised with clear margins. Marjolin ulcers can be prevented with early excision and grafting of burn wounds. The prognosis is poor with a high rate of recurrence.

SCC is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure.

Variants :

* Bowen's Disease

* Erythroplasia of Queyrat

SCC initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin.

Treatment:  Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Other modalities include cautery ablation, cryotherapy, drug therapy including imiquimod, Moh’s microsurgery and Radiation therapy.

Other options:

Option A: A malignancy cannot be incised. Some malignancies can have local control through wide local excision.

Option C: Squamous cell carcinomas spread lymphatogenously.

Option D: Chronic antibiotic therapy is not recommended for SCC. It is used in the treatment of chronic osteomyelitis, actinomycosis and tuberculosis.

Pearl PF0158: Marjolin’s Ulcer

* Low-grade cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising from

* Long-standing ulcer like venous ulcer

* Post-burn scar

* Chronic osteomyelitis

* Post-radiation ulcer.

* Slow progression to malignancy (SCC) since it is relatively avascular.

* Painless due to the absence of nerves in scar tissue.

* No secondary deposits since there are no lymphatics in scar tissue.

* Radioresistant due to avascularity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman came to the OPD with a diagnosis of advanced cervical cancer. She has a 14-year-old daughter. What advice would you give for her daughter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Advise HPV vaccine

Most cases of cervical cancer are caused by Human Papillomavirus infection.

High-risk oncogenic types include:

• HPV 16
• HPV 18

These account for \~70% of cervical cancers.

| Age group | Schedule

| --------- | --------

| 9–14 years | 2 doses (0 and 6 months)

| ≥15 years | 3 doses

Best time for HPV vaccination is before sexual debut.

Since the daughter is 14 years old, she falls into the ideal vaccination age group.

At 14 years, the best preventive strategy is HPV vaccination (primary prevention). Screening with Pap/HPV testing starts later (usually ≥25 years). BRCA/PTEN mutations are linked to other cancers, not typical cervical carcinoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During spermatogenesis, the process in which sperm cells develop from spermatogonia in the testes, the secretion of FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) in a male is inhibited by which factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibin

The secretion of FSH in a male is inhibited by negative feedback effect of Inhibin secreted by sertoli cells.

* GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).

* FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells. This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary.

* LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH. Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female, diabetic patient presented with acute onset fever and chills. She also complains of pain in the right flank area. Urine examination revealed plenty of leukocytes with glycosuria. A CT scan of the abdomen is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Emphysematous pyelonephritis

The given CT scan shows an enlarged kidney with areas of necrosis and mottled areas of gas collection. This is suggestive of emphysematous pyelonephritis.

This condition is common in diabetics and refers to a severe form of pyelonephritis with characteristic gas formation within or around the kidneys. If not treated early, it may lead to fulminant sepsis and is associated with high mortality.

CT scan is the best modality for the diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis. The following diagnostic features are seen:

* Enlarged, destructed renal parenchyma

* Small bubbly or linear streaks of gas

* Fluid collections, with gas-fluid levels

* Focal necrotic areas with or without abscess
questions.learning: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — The given CT scan shows an enlarged kidney with areas of necrosis and mottled areas of gas collection. This is suggestive of emphysematous pyelonephritis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of appendiceal carcinoma is most frequently associated with the development of pseudomyxoma peritonei?
questions.explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is characterized by the accumulation of mucinous (jelly-like) material within the peritoneal cavity. It most commonly results from the rupture of a mucin-producing tumor of the appendix. The tumor most frequently responsible is a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the appendix. When this tumor ruptures, it releases mucin-secreting epithelial cells into the peritoneal cavity. These cells continue to produce mucin, leading to progressive accumulation and the characteristic “jelly belly” appearance. Although earlier terminology included mucinous cystadenoma, current understanding classifies most of these lesions under the spectrum of appendiceal mucinous neoplasms, with adenocarcinoma being the clinically significant and commonly tested answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Mucinous cystadenoma → Older term; less emphasized in exams (C) Carcinoid tumor → Neuroendocrine, non-mucinous (D) Serous cystadenoma → Typically ovarian, not appendiceal
questions.learning: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is characterized by the accumulation of mucinous (jelly-like) material within the peritoneal cavity. It most commonly results from the rupture of a mucin-producing tumor of the appendix.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For which of the following procedures in the given OT list, can you preferably do a hysteroscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asherman syndrome

Of the following procedures given in the OT list, Asherman syndrome is the condition for which hysteroscopy would be most preferable. Hysteroscopy is used for the definitive diagnosis of Asherman syndrome.

Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of adhesion within the endometrial cavity. It is also called uterine synechiae and can be asymptomatic tiny bands or can completely or almost completely obliterate the endometrial cavity. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous uterine curettage, tuberculous endometritis, pelvic radiation, or endometrial ablation.

Depending on the degree of scarring, patients may have amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or recurrent pregnancy loss because of inadequate placentation. Hysterosalpingography is performed to assess the uterine cavity and tubal patency. Intrauterine adhesions are characteristically seen as irregular angulated filling defects in the uterine cavity with a classic 'moth-eaten' appearance. Definitive diagnosis (gold standard) and management are done by hysteroscopy. Hysteroscopic transection is the surgical treatment of choice.

Hysteroscopy has the advantage of being a minimally invasive procedure with lower risks and faster recovery times than traditional open surgery. It is often performed as an outpatient procedure, and patients can usually return to their normal activities within a day or two.

Other options-

Option A - Tubal ligation is done to attain permanent contraception in females, which is usually accomplished by occlusion or division of the fallopian tubes. It prevents ovum passage and fertilization. Procedures done at the time of delivery are termed puerperal sterilization. For puerperal sterilization, suture ligation with tubal segment removal is more frequently employed. A tubal sterilization procedure done at a time unrelated to recent pregnancy is called non-puerperal tubal sterilization or interval sterilization. Currently, non-puerperal tubal sterilization is mainly accomplished via laparoscopy.

Option C - Endocercival polyps are mucinous columnar epithelium-covered benign endocervical stroma overgrowths. They often present as a single, elongated mass that is red, smooth, and projecting from the endocervical canal. Ring forceps are used to grab endocervical polyps for excision if the stalk is thin. The stalk base of the polyp is repeatedly twisted. Surgical ligation and excision of a thick pedicle may be necessary if further severe bleeding is expected. Although hysteroscopy can help visualize and assess these polyps, their removal is typically performed using forceps, either during a pelvic examination or during a colposcopy. Hysteroscopy is not the primary method for managing endocervical polyps.

Option D - Subserosal fibroids carry higher risks for incomplete resection, difficult visualization, or uterine perforation with hysteroscopic myomectomy. Hence, a number of parameters are taken into consideration while choosing a surgical strategy for subserosa or intramural myomas. Successful results and low recurrence rates are seen after laparoscopic leiomyoma excision.
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome Of the following procedures given in the OT list, Asherman syndrome is the condition for which hysteroscopy would be most preferable.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A boy with a history of a fall from a tree presents with a lurching gait and dragging of his feet. Which of the following structures are involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius (marked as 2).

The gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines. Insertion of the muscle is at the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

• When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
• The actions of these muscles are affected when there is an injury to the superior gluteal nerve, neck of the femur, or loss of normal angulation of the shaft of the femur. This occurs in conditions like paralysis of the glutei, developmental dysplasia of the hip, etc.
• When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb. This leads to a positive Trendelenburg's sign with a characteristic lurching gait - the patient lurches towards the affected side with contralateral pelvis drop.

Other options

1 - Gluteus maximus - involved in the extension of flexed thigh, abduction (only upper fibres), and lateral rotation at the hip joint. Insertion is at the iliotibial tract.

3 - Piriformis - involved in lateral rotation and assists abduction at the hip joint. It is inserted into the medial side of greater trochanter of the femur. Entrapment of the sciatic nerve in the piriformis can lead to piriformis syndrome.

4 - Sciatic nerve - The nerve passes over the obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior and quadratus femoris. It supplies knee flexors and muscles below the knee. Paralysis of this nerve results in flail foot and severe difficulty in walking.
questions.learning: 2 The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius (marked as 2). The gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is not true according to case-control study?
questions.explanation: A case-control study is a retrospective observational study design. It begins by identifying individuals who already have the outcome/disease (cases) and comparing them to those without it (controls). Therefore, it moves backward from the effect to the cause (Option A). Because researchers start with existing cases, this design is the most efficient and preferred method for studying rare diseases (Option B). The standard measure of association calculated in a case-control study is the Odds Ratio (Option C). The statement "Cause to effect" (Option D) is NOT true for case-control studies; instead, it describes a cohort study, which follows an exposed group over time to see who develops the disease. Understanding these directional differences is critical for selecting the appropriate study design for an epidemiologic investigation and interpreting its results correctly
questions.learning: A case-control study is a retrospective observational study design. It begins by identifying individuals who already have the outcome/disease (cases) and comparing them to those without it (controls).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A fetus recovered from a water canal has a crown–heel length of 25 cm. Based on this measurement, what is the approximate gestational age of the fetus?
questions.explanation: According to Haase’s Rule, fetal age can be estimated from crown–heel length: For the first 5 months of gestation: Age in months = √(length in cm) In this case: √25 = 5 months After 5 months: Age in months = length (cm) ÷ 5 (e.g., a 6-month fetus ≈ 30 cm) Why other options are incorrect: 6 months → expected length ≈ 30 cm 4 months → expected length ≈ 16 cm 3 months → expected length ≈ 9 cm

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient presents to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath and tiredness. There is no history of reactive airway disease or heart diseases previously. She has a history of breast cancer for which breast conservation surgery and chemoradiation were done. On examination, there were engorged neck veins and JVP showed rapid x and y descent and Chest Xray is as below.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The clinical features and the JVP findings of rapid X and Y descent  are suggestive of constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive pericarditis:

* It is the condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart.

* In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition.

* Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes.

* Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic.

* Clinically the patients present with dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue.

* JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures.

Diagnosis:

* Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations

* Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function.

* The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline.

* Echo can assess the hemodynamic function but it is accurate in identifying pericardial thickening.

* CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations.

* CT has an edge over MRI as it can detect calcification associated with this condition.

* Pericardial thickness of > 4mm along with clinical features of constriction is highly suggestive of this diagnosis.

* Cardiac MR may show diastolic septal bounce.

* Hepatomegaly and ascites can be seen associated with this condition.

Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration.

Other important conditions and their JVP tracings are

* In Cardiac tamponade, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) tracing of the patient will have a prominent x descent but an absent y descent.

* Atrioventricular block will have cannon a waves

* Atrial fibrillation will have absent a wave

* Tricuspid regurgitation will have accentuated v wave with rapid y descent

* Tricuspid stenosis will have prolonged y wave

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prominent a-waves
Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

Cannon a-waves

Complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial/ junctional/ ventricular beats

Absent a-waves
Atrial fibrillation

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

Abnormality
Conditions

Absent x-descent
Severe tricuspid regurgitation

Rapid x-descent
Cardiac tamponade

4) The v-wave corresponds to the venous filling of right atrium.

Abnormality
Conditions

Dominant v-waves
Tricuspid regurgitation

5) The y-descent corresponds to the passive emptying of the right atrium into right ventricle.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prolonged y-descent
Tricuspid stenosis

Rapid y-descent

Constrictive pericarditis and isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation

Absent y-descent
Cardiac tamponade

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4 day old baby is active and feeding well. He has a bilirubin level of 8 mg/dl. What is the next step in the management of the baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continue breastfeeding

Since this child has a bilirubin level of only 8 mg/dl on the 4th day, it points to physiologic jaundice. The child is active and feeding well, the mother should be encouraged to continue breastfeeding frequently and exclusively.

All the other options would be possible treatment choices if the child had pathological jaundice.

Physiological jaundice/Icterus neonatorum is due to increased bilirubin production from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells combined with transient limitation in the conjugation of bilirubin by the immature neonatal liver. It first appears on the 2nd or 3rd days usually peaks on the 4th day at 5-6 mg/dL and decreases to <2 mg/dL between the 5th and 7th days after birth.

On the other hand, in pathological jaundice, appearance is within the first 24 hours after birth and may be present at or beyond the age of 2 weeks in term babies and 3 weeks in preterms babies. There may be an elevated direct (or conjugated) bilirubin level. Jaundice visible on the palms and soles, unresponsiveness to phototherapy, and a rapid rise in bilirubin levels during phototherapy indicate pathological jaundice.

Phototherapy is initiated in babies with pathological jaundice when the bilirubin levels exceed the 95th percentile on the total serum bilirubin (TSB) normogram. Babies are kept at a distance of 30-45 cm from the UV lamp (460-490 nm) with eyes and gonads covered. It is avoided in babies with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to the risk of bronze-baby syndrome. Dehydration and hypocalcemia are potential complications and breastfeeding is encouraged.

Exchange transfusion (ET) is done in cases of bilirubin encephalopathy, Rh incompatibility with significant hemolysis, and bilirubin values exceeding TSB cutoffs for ET.
questions.learning: Continue breastfeeding Since this child has a bilirubin level of only 8 mg/dl on the 4th day, it points to physiologic jaundice. The child is active and feeding well, the mother should be encouraged to continue breastfeeding frequently and exclusively.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerve nuclei is not a part of the special visceral afferent (SVA) column?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trochlear nerve

The trochlear nerve nucleus is a part of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column, not the special visceral afferent column.

The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that innervates superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

The neurons of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column innervate the extrinsic ocular muscles and muscles of the tongue (III, IV, VI, and XII cranial nerves).
questions.learning: Trochlear nerve — The trochlear nerve nucleus is a part of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column, not the special visceral afferent column. The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that innervates superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with a chronic tingling sensation in the forearm. A neurological examination is done and appears to be normal. Which of the following receptors are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pacinian corpuscles-fast vibration

Pacinian corpuscles are responsible for sensing fast vibration. The chronic tingling sensation is mediated by pressure-sensitive Aβ fibers and low-conduction velocity C fibers.

Pacinian corpuscles are the most sensitive mechanoreceptors in the somatosensory system. They are responsive to high-frequency (30–500 Hz) vibratory stimuli and deep pressure. They are also examples of rapidly adapting receptors.

Chronic tingling causing conditions include Diabetes, carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar nerve palsy, radial nerve palsy, tarsal tunnel syndrome, sciatica, vitamin B1,B6,B12 deficiencies, and alcoholism.

Other options

Option A: The Merkel cells are expanded dendritic endings in the epidermis of glabrous skin and respond to sustained pressure and touch.

Option B: Meissner's corpuscle senses tap and flutter. They are present in dermal papillae. They are rapidly adapting receptors.

Option D: Ruffini's corpuscles are enlarged dendritic endings with elongated capsules in the dermis of glabrous and hairy skin. They respond to stretch and fluttering vibrations. They are slowly adapting receptors.
questions.learning: Pacinian corpuscles-fast vibration Pacinian corpuscles are responsible for sensing fast vibration. The chronic tingling sensation is mediated by pressure-sensitive Aβ fibers and low-conduction velocity C fibers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Ga-68 PSMA PET scan is used to diagnose which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) PET scanning is a specialized and highly sensitive imaging modality used specifically for the diagnosis and staging of prostate cancer. PSMA is a protein that is overexpressed on the surface of most prostate cancer cells. The Ga-68 tracer binds specifically to this protein, allowing for the detection of even very small areas of cancerous tissue. It is particularly valuable for detecting localized recurrence or metastatic disease when traditional scans like bone scans or CT are negative or inconclusive. Lung cancer (Option A), colon cancer (Option C), and liver cancer (Option D) are typically staged with other modalities, most commonly FDG-PET or contrast-enhanced CT. PSMA-PET has revolutionized the management of prostate cancer by providing more accurate staging, which guides the choice between radical surgery, radiation, or systemic therapies
questions.learning: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) PET scanning is a specialized and highly sensitive imaging modality used specifically for the diagnosis and staging of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fossa of Rosenmuller

The image shown is the endoscopic view of lateral wall of the nasopharynx, and the marked structure is the fossa of Rosenmuller.

The nasopharynx is present above the soft palate and is made up of the roof, floor, posterior wall, and two lateral walls.

Important structures seen in the nasopharynx are

• Pharyngeal opening of the eustachian tube
• Torus tubarius- tubal elevation which is present behind the opening of the eustachian tube.
• Fossa of Rosenmuller - A lateral pharyngeal recess that is present above and behind the torus tubarius. It is the most common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
• Adenoids or nasopharyngeal tonsil, which is present in the roof and posterior wall
• Passavant's ridge

The tubal tonsil is a collection of subepithelial lymphoid tissue situated at the tubal elevation. It is a part of the Waldeyer’s ring and infection can cause eustachian tube occlusion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 15-month-old child with severe acute malnutrition presents with acute watery diarrhea. The child is irritable, has sunken eyes, and drinks eagerly when offered water. According to IMCI criteria, how should the dehydration be classified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Some dehydration

According to the WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, some dehydration is diagnosed when a child with diarrhea has two or more of the following signs:

• Restless or irritable
• Sunken eyes
• Drinks eagerly/thirsty
• Skin pinch goes back slowly

| IMCI Classification | Clinical Features | Management

| ------------------- | ----------------- | ----------

| No dehydration | <2 signs | Plan A (home fluids + zinc)

| Some dehydration ⭐ | ≥2 of: restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch slow | Plan B (ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours)

| Severe dehydration | ≥2 of: lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly/unable to drink, skin pinch very slow | Plan C (IV fluids)

Why not the other options?

• A. No dehydration – The child would have fewer than two signs of dehydration.
• C. Severe dehydration – Requires two or more of the following: lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, not able to drink or drinking poorly, and skin pinch returning very slowly.
• D. Shock – Characterized by cold extremities, weak rapid pulse, prolonged capillary refill time, and hypotension; these are not IMCI dehydration categories

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which lymph node is most commonly involved in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pelvic

The most common lymph node of metastatic disease in prostate cancer is the pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the pelvic, obturator, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.
questions.learning: Pelvic — The most common lymph node of metastatic disease in prostate cancer is the pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a child presenting with abdominal distension, pallor, lethargy, exclusive feeding on rice water, and laboratory findings of reduced serum protein and albumin levels?
questions.explanation: The child’s presentation of a swollen abdomen (pitting edema), lethargy (unenergetic expression), and a history of being fed exclusively rice water (high in carbohydrates but deficient in protein) is indicative of Kwashiorkor. In this form of severe acute malnutrition, low dietary protein leads to hypoalbuminemia (decreased serum protein and albumin), which reduces plasma oncotic pressure and results in generalized edema and abdominal distension. Marasmus (Option B) is characterized by a global deficiency of all calories, leading to severe wasting and an "old man" facial appearance without significant edema. Indian childhood cirrhosis (Option C) typically involves liver failure in older children. Kawasaki disease (Option D) is an acute vasculitis characterized by high fever and skin changes, not nutritional edema. Therefore, the specific combination of a high-carbohydrate/low-protein diet and hypoalbuminemic edema confirms the diagnosis of Kwashiorkor
questions.learning: The child’s presentation of a swollen abdomen (pitting edema), lethargy (unenergetic expression), and a history of being fed exclusively rice water (high in carbohydrates but deficient in protein) is indicative of Kwashiorkor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor of adequacy of shock therapy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urine output

Urine output is the most reliable bedside indicator of end-organ perfusion and the best clinical monitor of adequacy of shock resuscitation. Since the kidneys are highly sensitive to hypoperfusion, restoration of adequate urine output reflects successful improvement in renal blood flow, cardiac output, and tissue perfusion. Target urine output:

• Adults: ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour
• Children: ≥1 mL/kg/hour
• Burn patients: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour (adults), 1 mL/kg/hour (children)

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Central venous pressure (CVP): CVP reflects right atrial pressure/preload, but is a poor predictor of tissue perfusion or fluid responsiveness.
• B. Pulmonary wedge pressure (PCWP): PCWP estimates left ventricular filling pressure and is mainly used in selected critically ill patients; it is not the best routine monitor of shock resuscitation.
• D. Restoring blood pressure/pulse vital parameters: Normal blood pressure and pulse do not necessarily indicate adequate tissue perfusion, as compensatory mechanisms may maintain vital signs despite ongoing organ hypoperfusion.
questions.learning: Urine output Urine output is the most reliable bedside indicator of end-organ perfusion and the best clinical monitor of adequacy of shock resuscitation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 53-year-old patient was brought to the emergency room with altered sensorium and rapid shallow breathing. His abdomen is distended with palpable hepatomegaly and splenomegaly and sclerae are icteric. The other examination findings are given below. Laboratory tests show that the AST: ALT ratio is 3:1. What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alcoholic liver disease

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with altered consciousness, jaundice (scleral icterus), and signs of liver cirrhosis (distended abdomen, hepatomegaly), spider naevi, Terry nails, and the characteristic AST>ALT is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease.

In alcoholic liver disease, the AST:ALT ratio is typically >2:1. A ratio of >3:1 is strongly supportive and seen in significant alcohol-related liver injury.

The ratio is due to the deficiency of pyridoxal 5’-phosphate seen in alcoholics. It is a cofactor needed for ALT activity.

* Aspartate transaminase (AST) - 10-40 IU/L

* Alanine transaminase (ALT) - 10-40 IU/L

The AST:ALT ratio can be interpreted as follows:

Condition

Suggestive of alcoholic liver disease

Alcohol intake is associated with the deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate, which in turn leads to decreased levels of ALT enzyme. So, AST>ALT.

Other options:

Option B: In acute viral hepatitis, the aminotransferases are often elevated > 500 IU (400-4000 IU/L) due to extensive cell injury.

Option C: In autoimmune hepatitis, aminotransferase levels are elevated and fluctuate in the range of 100-1000 IU/L. Autoimmune hepatitis may present as acute or chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis. Commonly associated symptoms include fatigue, anorexia, pruritis, arthralgias, upper abdominal discomfort, and skin rashes including acne among others.

Option D: Acute acetaminophen poisoning (paracetamol tablets ingestion).In acute acetaminophen poisoning, the aminotransferases are elevated > 1000 IU and may exceed 10,000 IU/L due to acute hepatocellular injury.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents after a motorcycle road traffic accident with no reported pain or injury. During examination, blood is observed at the tip of the urethral meatus, and the bladder is non-palpable. What would be your next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wait for bladder to fill

The given clinical scenario showing blood at the tip of the urethral meatus following a road traffic accident (RTA) is a clinical hallmark of a urethral injury. The next best step in this scenario is to wait and watch.

Injuries to the urethra are more common in males. They are of:

Part of the urethra
Injury type
Clinical features

Bulbar urethra
(distal urethral injury)
Blunt trauma to the perineum
Butterfly hematoma (perineal bruising), urinary retention, and bleeding from the urethral tip

Bulbomembranous junction
(proximal urethral injury)
Road traffic accidents
Blood at the tip of the meatus and urinary retention
High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)

Retrograde urethrography using water-soluble contrast is used for localizing the site of urethral injury.

The patient should be managed with analgesia and antibiotics. If the bladder is full, it should be drained with a catheter placed by percutaneous suprapubic puncture using a Seldinger technique.

Other options:

Option A: Foley catheterization should not be done since it might convert a partial tear into a complete tear.

Option C: Nephrogram is not done but retrograde urethrogram is performed in urethral injury.

Option D: Suprapubic Cystostomy is done only in cases where the bladder is full or the patient is unable to urinate following a pelvic fracture/ RTA.
questions.learning: Wait for bladder to fill — The given clinical scenario showing blood at the tip of the urethral meatus following a road traffic accident (RTA) is a clinical hallmark of a urethral injury.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with continuous discomfort in the right hypochondrium. Upon examination, an enlarged liver 8cm below the costal margins is noted. The image below displays his CT radiograph. Additionally, he reports a history of spending a significant amount of time around pet dogs. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Echinococcus granulosus

The given clinical scenario along with  CT scan of the liver showing a hydatid cyst seen as a hypodense lesion with internal septation, suggests a diagnosis of Echinococcus granulosus. It is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Hydatid cysts result from infection by the Echinococcus, and can result in cyst formation anywhere in the body.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

Investigation:

* CT examination reveals a fluid density cyst, with frequent peripheral focal areas of calcification, which usually indicates no active infection if completely circumferential.

* Septation and daughter cysts may be visualised. The water-lily sign indicates a cyst with a floating, undulating membrane, caused by a detached endocyst.

* May also show hyperdense internal septa representing a spoke wheel pattern within a cyst.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with complaints of nocturnal pruritus. Examination shows burrows over intertriginous areas, axilla, umbilicus, and in between the digits. Which of the following vectors is responsible for transmitting this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoptes scabiei

The given clinical history of nocturnal pruritis and borrows over intertriginous areas, axilla, umbilicus, and in between digits is suggestive of scabies. It is caused by the itch mite also called Sarcoptes scabiei.

Scabies is caused by an infestation of Sarcoptes scabiei. It is transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact and less frequently via contaminated clothes and bedding. They are seen more commonly in overcrowded areas, hostels, and schools, especially in unhygienic environments.

Clinically, these patients present with superficial excoriated papules or vesicles that are intensely pruritic. They are usually present on the volar surface of the wrists, interdigital spaces, penis, scrotum, navel, and skin folds and creases in the axillae, buttocks, and thigh regions. Burrows may be visualized in the superficial dermis in the above mentioned regions. Pruritis is typically intense and increases after showers and during the night.

Diagnosis is established considering the characteristic history and by dermatoscopic imaging or microscopy of the skin scrapings or cellophane tape lifted from lesions.

Permethrin cream - 5% is the treatment of choice. It is preferred over 1% lindane preparation and ivermectin. These preparations are applied once, all over the body below the jawline, following a bath. It should be washed off with soap and water after 8-14 hours.

It is imperative to treat close contacts simultaneously and wash bedding and clothing to prevent reinfestations.

The image given below shows itch mite.

Other options:

Option A: Crab louse infestation causes pediculosis pubis.

Option C: Rat fleas are vectors for endemic typhus, bubonic plague, and hymenolepis diminuta.

Option D: Ixodes ticks (hard ticks) transmit rocky mountain spotted fever, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, Colorado tick fever, tularemia, tick paralysis, and human babesiosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman presents with vault prolapse. It is being fixed to a bony point with a mesh. Where is this mesh fixed to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sacral promontory

In sacrohysteropexy, the mesh is attached from the cervix/uterus to the sacral promontory, providing strong apical support. Ischial structures are not used for mesh fixation. Gold standard surgery for vault prolapse = sacrocolpopexy.

The Sacral Promontory provides:

| --------- | ------

| Strong fixation | Firm bony landmark

| Restores vaginal axis | Anatomical alignment

| Durable repair | Low recurrence rate

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male presents with 2 weeks of cough, fever and night sweats. Investigations reveal a CD4 count of 100 /μL. Which of the following infections is most likely to be seen in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycobacterium avium complex

The clinical vignette suggests opportunistic infection in HIV patients. The most common opportunistic infection when CD4 counts falls below 100 is disseminated mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections

Mycobacterium avium complex, or Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex, is a group of slow-growing, nonchromogenic non-tuberculous mycobacteria. The infections occur in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. It is the most frequent organism affecting HIV and immunosuppressed patients, although about 40% of pulmonary infections occur in immunocompetent patients. Cervical lymphadenitis is the most common presentation in young children of age <5 years. Other manifestations include skin, and soft tissue infections, musculoskeletal infections, and disseminated disease

Treatment with either clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol is a preferred initial therapy along with starting anti-retroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is classically seen in the histopathology of the following?
questions.explanation: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is a pathognomonic histopathological term used to describe Hailey-Hailey disease (Benign Familial Pemphigus) (Option A) . This genetic disorder is characterized by widespread acantholysis (loss of cell-to-cell adhesion) throughout the entire epidermis. On microscopy, the partially detached keratinocytes resemble a crumbling or dilapidated wall. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B) also features acantholysis but it is typically suprabasal, resulting in a "tombstone" appearance of the basal layer. Darier’s disease (Option C) is characterized by dyskeratosis with "corps ronds" and "grains." Bullous pemphigoid (Option D) involves a subepidermal split without acantholysis. Because the "dilapidated wall" specifically describes the extensive, irregular epidermal detachment seen in this familial condition, Hailey-Hailey is the definitive diagnosis. It typically presents with recurrent blisters and erosions in the skin folds (axilla/groin). Understanding these distinct histological patterns is crucial for differentiating various immunobullous and genetic skin disorders
questions.learning: The "dilapidated brick wall" appearance is a pathognomonic histopathological term used to describe Hailey-Hailey disease (Benign Familial Pemphigus) (Option A) .

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Paralysis of which muscle causes ptosis in Horner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superior tarsal muscle

Ptosis in Horner syndrome is due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle, which is a sympathetically innervated smooth muscle.

This causes mild ptosis, unlike complete ptosis from levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) palsy.

Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid, and orbitalis has no role in eyelid elevation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man is referred from the infertility clinic to the surgical OPD after palpation reveals a “bag of worms” sensation along with dilated veins in the scrotum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The pathognomonic physical finding of a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum is diagnostic of a Varicocele. This condition involves the abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins in the pampiniform plexus. It is most commonly found on the left side due to the anatomical drainage of the left spermatic vein into the renal vein. Varicoceles are a leading cause of correctable male infertility because the blood pooling increases scrotal temperature, which impairs spermatogenesis. Testicular torsion (Option C) is an acute surgical emergency presenting with sudden, severe pain. Hydrocele (Option A) presents as a painless, transilluminant fluid collection. Epididymo-orchitis (Option D) is an inflammatory condition characterized by acute pain, swelling, and often fever. Given the specific context of the infertility clinic referral and the characteristic "bag of worms" palpation, varicocele is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves surgical ligation or embolization of the dilated veins
questions.learning: The pathognomonic physical finding of a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum is diagnostic of a Varicocele. This condition involves the abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins in the pampiniform plexus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 59-year-old lady presents with a progressive painless lump in the breast. What is the cause for the following skin change?
options: Spread of tumor to anterior chest wall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infiltration of subdermal lymphatics

The image shows the peau d'orange appearance and it occurs due to the infiltration of the subdermal lymphatics.

Peau d'orange appearance is a skin change in which the skin of the breast appears like that of an orange. It is due to cutaneous lymphatic edema caused by dermal lymphatic infiltration by malignant cells. It is seen in several conditions such as:

• inflammatory carcinoma of the breast
• mastitis
• chronic abscess
• following breast surgery or radiation

Other options:

Option B: Infiltration of lactiferous duct leads to nipple retraction.

Option C: Involvement of Cooper's ligament leads to dimpling of the skin over the breast.

Option D: In case of spread of the tumor to the anterior chest wall, the breast will appear fixed and will not fall forwards when bending. On lifting the arm above the shoulder, the breast will not move upward.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for a newborn with weak lower limb pulses and strong upper limb pulses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coarctation of Aorta

Coarctation of the aorta will be the diagnosis for a newborn with weak lower-limb pulses and strong upper-limb pulses.

Coarctation refers to a constriction or narrowing in the aorta, which can be proximal or distal to the ductus arteriosus. CoA usually presents either in infancy or in later childhood as incidental upper limb hypertension and disparity of pulses in the upper  and lower limbs as radio-femoral delay.

When the ductus arteriosus is open in an infant with severe coarctation, the left-to-right shunt established during birth across the ductus arteriosus during birth is reversed to a right-to-left shunt as there is coarctation above the ductus in the aorta. This leads to deoxygenated blood flow to the lower limbs and no change in pulse in the lower limbs. As the ductus arteriosus closes, there is a pooling of blood in the heart, leading to congestive heart failure, further leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance as well as lack of blood flow to lower limbs (presenting as weak pulses in the lower extremities).

Figure of 3 sign is pathognomonic of coarctation of the aorta. Prestenotic dilatation of the aortic arch and left subclavian artery, indentation at the coarctation site and post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta combine to form this sign.

Treatment includes re-establishing patency of the ductus arteriosus by prostaglandin E1 infusion and heart failure medical management followed by definitive surgical management such as coarctectomy, end-to-end anastomosis, or patch aortoplasty. Restenosis of CoA areas later in childhood are common and are treated by balloon angioplasty.

Other options:

Option A: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart disease encountered beyond the age of 1 year. It is characterized by a tetrad of:

* Severe right ventricle outflow obstruction

* Large ventricular septal defect (VSD)

* Aorta overriding VSD

* Right ventricular hypertrophy

Option C:  Transposition of great arteries (TGA) is a cyanotic congenital anomaly where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, resulting in systemic and pulmonary circulations existing as two parallel circuits. Survival in the immediate neonatal period is due to the mixture of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood provided by the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. About half of the patients also have a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Clinical manifestations become apparent soon after birth, with infants presenting with cyanosis and tachypnea. It is associated with moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.

Option D: Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets. A box-shaped heart is seen in Ebstein's anomaly. There is severe right-sided cardiomegaly due to an elongated and enlarged right atrium, which leads to an elevated apex.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man develops chest tightness, shortness of breath, and altered consciousness while undertaking a high-altitude mountain pilgrimage. Which intervention would provide symptomatic relief in this situation?
questions.explanation: The patient is likely suffering from High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE) or severe Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS). The primary intervention for providing relief and facilitating acclimatization is Acetazolamide. It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that induces a mild metabolic acidosis by increasing renal bicarbonate excretion. This acidosis stimulates the respiratory centers in the medulla to increase ventilation, thereby counteracting the low atmospheric oxygen levels. Mannitol (Option A) is an osmotic diuretic used for cerebral edema in other contexts but is not the standard for high-altitude illness. Digoxin (Option B) and Diltiazem (Option C) are cardiac medications with no role in high-altitude relief. For patients with severe HACE or High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE), the absolute most critical intervention is immediate descent to a lower altitude and supplemental oxygen. Dexamethasone is often added to acetazolamide for HACE to reduce brain swelling. Acetazolamide remains the foundational pharmacological tool for both preventing and treating high-altitude sickness in trekkers and pilgrims
questions.learning: The patient is likely suffering from High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE) or severe Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS). The primary intervention for providing relief and facilitating acclimatization is Acetazolamide.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A man is found 100 km away from home, confused about identity and travel, after an earthquake. No head injury or substance use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dissociative fugue

Dissociative fugue involves sudden travel, amnesia for the period, and identity confusion, often triggered by trauma. Dissociative amnesia lacks travel, DID involves multiple identities, and schizophrenia presents differently.

questions.text: A child presents with periorbital oedema and pedal oedema. The laboratory investigations reveal serum creatinine = 2.1 mg/dL, urinary protein: 5.2 g/day, and Cholesterol: 310 mg/dL. Which of the following are included in the criteria of diagnosis of Nephrotic syndrome? 1. Proteinuria >3.5 g/day 2. Hyperlipidemia 3. Creatinine more than 1.5mg/dl 4. Hypoalbuminaemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Core Diagnostic Criteria of Nephrotic Syndrome

| Criterion | Mechanism

| --------- | ---------

| Proteinuria >3.5 g/day | Increased glomerular permeability

| Hypoalbuminemia | Loss of albumin in urine

| Hyperlipidemia | Liver compensatory synthesis

| Edema | ↓ oncotic pressure + Na retention

Nephrotic syndrome is defined by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) leading to hypoalbuminemia, which in turn causes edema and secondary hyperlipidemia.

Serum creatinine is not part of the diagnostic criteria and may be normal or elevated depending on renal function.

| --------- | --------------------- | -----------

| 1. Proteinuria >3.5 g/day | ✅ | Hallmark feature

| 2. Hyperlipidemia | ✅ | Liver compensation

| 3. Creatinine | ❌ | Reflects renal function, not definition

| 4. Hypoalbuminemia | ✅ | Due to urinary loss

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Primary follicles arrest in which phase of prophase 1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diplotene

The correct answer is Diplotene.

Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

This arrest is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) and meiosis resumes only at ovulation.

Leptotene, zygotene, and pachytene are earlier phases of prophase I that do not show physiological arrest.

questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent headaches and a family history of early sudden cardiac deaths. On examination, he has hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and arterial tortuosity. Echocardiography reveals aortic root dilatation. Genetic testing shows a mutation affecting the TGF-β signaling pathway. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: C. Loeys–Dietz syndrome

Loeys–Dietz syndrome is caused by mutations in the TGF-β signaling pathway and is characterized by hypertelorism, bifid uvula/cleft palate, arterial tortuosity, and early aggressive aortic root dilatation, explaining the family history of sudden cardiac death.

A. Marfan syndrome – FBN1 mutation; lacks bifid uvula and arterial tortuosity.

B. Vascular Ehlers–Danlos – COL3A1 mutation; features translucent skin, not craniofacial anomalies.

D. Homocystinuria – Marfanoid habitus with intellectual disability and thrombosis, not TGF-β mutation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Alcohol abuse is strongly associated with the development of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dilated cardiomyopathy

Alcohol abuse is strongly associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Alcohol and its metabolites, especially acetaldehyde have a direct toxic effect on the myocardium which leads to the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy:

• Acquired causes :

• Infectious and non-infectious myocarditis: most common cause globally
• Alcohol is the most common cause in India
• Pregnancy:

• Pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy (PACM)
• Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM)

• Stress-induced: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
• Drug-induced:

• Doxorubicin (anthracycline)
• Trastuzumab
• Cyclophosphamide

• Nutritional deficiency:

• Beriberi (thiamine),
• Keshan disease (selenium),
• Carnitine deficiency

• Endocrine: Hypo and hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, diabetes mellitus
• Others:

• Cobalt toxicity,
• Heavy metals (lead, mercury, arsenic, lithium)

• Familial causes (50%):

• Mutation in the cardiac myocyte titin gene
• Haemochromatosis
• Syndromes: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Becker’s muscular dystrophy

questions.text: Which of the following vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:

The live attenuated varicella virus vaccine is currently recommended for children between 12 to 18 months of age who have not had chickenpox.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Based on the stool examination findings, what is the most likely cause of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea in a 6-year-old boy?
questions.explanation: The stool examination reveals a trophozoite containing an ingested red blood cell (erythrophagocytosis). This is the definitive diagnostic feature that distinguishes the pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica from the non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar. E. histolytica causes amoebic dysentery, characterized by abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Giardia lamblia (Option A) trophozoites have a characteristic "owl’s eye" appearance with flagella and cause watery, fatty stools, not dysentery. Shigella (Option B) and Campylobacter (Option D) are bacteria; while they cause bloody diarrhea, they would not appear as large amoebic trophozoites on a wet mount. The trophozoite of E. histolytica also shows a characteristic cartwheel-like nucleus. Ingested RBCs are pathognomonic for active, invasive amoebiasis. Treatment requires a nitroimidazole like metronidazole followed by a luminal amoebicide. Therefore, based on the microscopic evidence of erythrophagocytosis, Entamoeba histolytica is the most probable cause

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following structures is responsible for balance and hearing?
questions.explanation: The inner ear, also known as the labyrinth, houses the sensory organs for two distinct special senses. The vestibule (Option C) is the central part of the bony labyrinth and acts as a common chamber. It contains the utricle and saccule, which detect linear balance, and it communicates directly with the semicircular canals (Option A), which detect angular balance. The vestibule also connects to the cochlea (Option B), the structure responsible for hearing. While the cochlea is solely for hearing and the canals are solely for balance, the vestibule is the anatomical region associated with the housing of components for both functions. The Organ of Corti (Option D) is the specific sensory neuroepithelium for hearing located within the cochlea. Therefore, in a general anatomical context, the vestibule is the most appropriate collective answer for the site of both these senses. Damage to the labyrinth often causes concurrent vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss
questions.learning: The inner ear, also known as the labyrinth, houses the sensory organs for two distinct special senses. The vestibule (Option C) is the central part of the bony labyrinth and acts as a common chamber.

On examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye. questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following with regard to Amino Acids: I. Essential amino acids are those that the body cannot synthesize and they must be obtained from dietary proteins. II. Not just the essential amino acids, non-essential amino acids are also needed by the body for synthesis of tissue proteins. III. Unless a protein contains all the essential amino acids in amounts corresponding to human needs, a protein is said to be biologically incomplete. IV. Animal proteins are rated superior to vegetable proteins. Of the above statements, how many are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All four

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are classified into essential and non-essential amino acids based on the body’s ability to synthesize them. The biological value (BV) of a protein depends on its content of essential amino acids and their proportion relative to human requirements.

• Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
• Non-essential amino acids can be synthesized by the body but are also required for protein synthesis and normal growth.
• A protein lacking one or more essential amino acids in adequate amounts is called a biologically incomplete protein.
• Animal proteins (milk, egg, meat, fish) are complete proteins with high biological value, whereas most vegetable proteins are incomplete.
questions.learning: All four Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are classified into essential and non-essential amino acids based on the body’s ability to synthesize them.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the given image, which type of injury is shown according to the Bismuth-Strasberg classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type A

Strasberg Type A bile duct injury : characterized by cystic duct leak or leak from small ducts in the gallbladder bed, is the most common type of acute bile duct injury.

Management: ERCP and CBD stenting as it does not involve major bile ducts.

Revise Strassberg-Bismuth classification:

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Type A | Bile leak from cystic duct stump or small ducts in gallbladder bed (ducts of Luschka); main biliary tree intact

| Type B | Occlusion of an aberrant right hepatic duct (usually mistakenly clipped/ligated) without bile leak

| Type C | Transection of an aberrant right hepatic duct with bile leak (duct not connected to common bile duct)

| Type D | Lateral injury to a major bile duct (partial tear of common bile duct or hepatic duct)

| Type E | Complete transection or stricture of major bile duct (equivalent to Bismuth classification)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the histopathological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amyloidosis

The given histopathological slide shows congo red staining that is used in staining amyloid.

Amyloidosis refers to extracellular deposits of fibrillar proteins. Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

It could be classified as systemic, localized, and hereditary amyloidosis. Microscopically, all types of amyloid deposits are made up of continuous, nonbranching fibrils. A characteristic cross-β-pleated sheet conformation is visualized on X-ray crystallography and infrared spectroscopy.

The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to the amyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy.

The image shows a congo-red stained biopsy specimen with the following:

(A) focal positive staining (orange-red) of amorphous extracellular material

(B) apple-green birefringence under polarized light

The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis using mass spectrometry.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In ocular surface examination and dry eye staining, which of the following order of dyes is used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorescein ->Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green

Amongst the given options, the better order of dyes to pick for use in ocular surface examination and dry eye staining is Fluorescein -> Rose Bengal -> Lisssamine green.

Fluorescein staining of the cornea is carried out with a disposable autoclaved filter paper strip impregnated with the dye. The denuded epithelial area seen in corneal abrasions or ulcers appears brilliant green when stained with fluorescein. Under a cobalt blue light, the stained area appears opaque green.

A corneal abrasion highlighted with fluorescein staining is shown below.

Rose Bengal stains dead and devitalized cells including mucous strands on ocular surface. The dye causes a stinging and burning sensation soon after instillation.

Lissamine green stains dead and degenerate cells, but does not stain healthy epithelial cells. It is used to diagnose ocular surface disease. It stains the conjunctiva. It does not cause stinging like Rose Bengal. The Green staining is best observed two minutes after instillation.

The image below shows the lissamine staining of the eye.

Note: The answer to this question is controversial and there is no clearcut evidence based information on the sequence. The above mentioned answer is the best amongst the given options based on consensus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Löfgren syndrome: 1. It is an acute illness and is more commonly seen in females. 2. It is a clinically distinct phenotype of sarcoidosis characterized by peripheral arthropathy and uveitis. 3. Clinical features include fever, erythema nodosum and bilateral lymphadenopathy. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 3 only

Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting presentation of sarcoidosis with an excellent prognosis. It is considered a distinct clinical phenotype of sarcoidosis and is seen more commonly in young females.

Löfgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis, good prognosis):

• Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
• Erythema nodosum
• Migratory polyarthralgia (ankles especially)
• ± Fever
• No uveitis or neuropathy in this triad — that's the trap

Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) — this is the one with uveitis

• Anterior uveitis
• Parotid gland enlargement
• Facial nerve palsy (cranial neuropathy, not peripheral)
• Fever

Neurosarcoidosis (general):

• Cranial neuropathies (CN VII most common)
• Can also cause peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex or symmetric polyneuropathy) — less classic than the cranial nerve involvement, but tested
• CNS involvement (mass lesions, meningitis, hypothalamic-pituitary axis)

questions.text: Spot the image.
questions.explanation: The image illustrates a Balloon Tamponade, a critical intervention for managing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) caused by uterine atony. Devices such as the Bakri balloon are inserted into the uterine cavity and inflated with fluid to provide mechanical compression against bleeding vessels in the uterine wall. An umbrella pack (Option B) is a surgical technique where a plastic bag filled with gauze is placed transabdominally to control pelvic bleeding after procedures like a hysterectomy. A parachute pack (Option C) is a variation of the umbrella pack that uses weighted pressure to control diffuse pelvic hemorrhage. Cervical ablation (Option D) is a treatment for precancerous lesions and has no role in the management of acute hemorrhage. Balloon tamponade is preferred as a first-line non-surgical option to stabilize patients and prevent the need for an emergency hysterectomy
