questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with vision problems and has a history of cataract surgery. OCT findings are given. What is the syndrome associated with these findings? OCT- Optical coherence tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irvine-Gass Syndrome

The given scenario of a patient with a history of cataract surgery and an OCT showing intraretinal cystoid spaces is suggestive of Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) in the setting of Irvine-Gass syndrome. It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region.

CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Irvine-Gass syndrome is the late postoperative complications of cataract surgery. The characteristic flower-petal appearance is due to the accumulation of dye in the outer plexiform layer at the fovea. CME occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and foveal depression. In advanced cases, a lamellar macular hole may develop.

Treatment includes topical anti-prostaglandins (ketorolac), steroids, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide), and managing the causative factor.

Given below is the FFA image showing the classic flower-petal appearance, followed by an OCT image showing intraretinal cystoid spaces in CME:

A few other late postoperative complications of cataract surgery include,

* Delayed chronic postoperative endophthalmitis

* Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy

* Retinal detachment

* After cataract or secondary cataract

Other options:

Option A: Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of the macular region neurosensory retina with/without retinal pigment epithelium detachment. Patients complain of sudden onset painless loss of vision, micropsia, and metamorphopsia. FFA shows two patterns of leakage, ink-blot pattern and smoke-stick pattern. OCT image of central serous retinopathy is seen below which neurosensory retinal detachment and accompanying small detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Option B: Posner–Schlossman syndrome is characterized by recurrent unilateral acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) (>40 mmHg) changes, with mild anterior uveitis. It is also known as glaucomatocyclitic crisis or hypertensive uveitis.

Option D: Elschnig’s pearls are where the subcapsular epithelial cells proliferate and develop into vacuolated soap bubble like clusters along the posterior capsule. It is a type of after-cataract/ secondary cataract or posterior capsular opacification, which is a late postoperative complication that follows extracapsular extraction of the lens.
questions.learning: Irvine-Gass Syndrome — The given scenario of a patient with a history of cataract surgery and an OCT showing intraretinal cystoid spaces is suggestive of Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) in the setting of Irvine-Gass syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true?
options: In a population with low prevalence of the disease, positive result with a highly sensitive test means true positive
Sensitivity depends on prevalence of the disease
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease
Specificity depends on prevalence of the disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease

The positive predictive value (PPV) of a screening test depends on the prevalence of the disease. The positive predictive value (PPV) of a test indicates the probability that a patient with a positive test result has actually contracted the disease i.e., the likelihood that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease.

If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the more accurate will be the positive predictive value. Therefore, in a population with a high prevalence of the disease, a positive result with a highly sensitive test means true positive. Example: Hypothyroidism is more prevalent in hilly areas than in coastal areas. If someone from a hilly area tests positive he is more likely to have the disease than someone who tests positive in a coastal area.

Likewise, if the prevalence decreases, the PPV will also become low. So in a population with a low prevalence of the disease, positive result with a highly sensitive test need not always mean true positive as it can produce an unacceptably high proportion of false positive results.

Predictive value is affected the most by prevalence. However, both sensitivity and specificity can change the predictive value.
questions.learning: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease The positive predictive value (PPV) of a screening test depends on the prevalence of the disease.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 40 year old female with burns over her abdomen, both limbs and back and presented after 8 hours. Which of the following is the formula for calculation of fluid infusion?
options: 2 ml/kg X %TBSA for the next 16 hours
5 ml/kg X %TSBA for the next 16 hours
4 ml/kg X %TSBA for first 8 hours then 2 ml/kg X %TBSA for next 16 hours
4 ml/kg X%TSBA for the next 16 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 ml/kg X %TBSA for the next 16 hours

Fluid resuscitation in burns:

According to ATLS 10th edition, 2018, the resuscitation formula used in thermal burns is 2 mL/kg × % TBSA.

First 8 hours: 1 mL/kg × % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution)
Next 16 hours: 1 mL/kg × % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution)

For a patient presenting 8 hours after sustaining thermal burns, the total volume using resuscitation formula should be given in the next 16 hours i.e; 2 mL/kg × % TBSA in the next 16 hours while maintaining target urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults.

In adults, urine output should be maintained between 30 and 50 cc/hr to minimize potential over-resuscitation.

Note:

The goal of resuscitation is to maintain the fine balance of adequate perfusion as indicated by urine output. It is important to understand that formulas provide a starting target rate; subsequently, the amount of fluids provided should be adjusted based on a urine output target of 0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults and 1 mL/kg/hr for children weighing less than 30 kg.

Total percentage of the burnt area is calculated clinically using the rule of nines.
questions.learning: 2 ml/kg X %TBSA for the next 16 hours Fluid resuscitation in burns: According to ATLS 10th edition, 2018, the resuscitation formula used in thermal burns is 2 mL/kg × % TBSA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with acute severe asthma shows poor response to nebulized salbutamol alone. After adding IV corticosteroids, bronchodilator responsiveness improves significantly within hours — too quickly to be explained by anti-inflammatory effects alone. What is the most likely mechanism for this rapid synergy?
options: Corticosteroids directly stimulate β-2 receptors as partial agonists
Corticosteroids increase transcription of β-2 receptor genes and prevent receptor desensitization
Corticosteroids inhibit phosphodiesterase, mimicking theophylline's action
Corticosteroids block muscarinic receptors, synergizing with β-2 agonists
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corticosteroids increase transcription of β-2 receptor genes and prevent receptor desensitization

Corticosteroids enhance bronchial responsiveness to β-2 agonists like salbutamol by increasing transcription of β-2 receptor genes, stabilizing their mRNA, and preventing receptor desensitization (tachyphylaxis) — a genomic effect that can manifest relatively quickly in the context of ongoing receptor turnover. This is distinct from their slower anti-inflammatory actions (reducing mucous secretion and inflammatory cell response). Steroids do not directly activate β-2 receptors (A), do not act through phosphodiesterase inhibition like theophylline (C), and have no direct antimuscarinic action (D).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the correct type of facial nerve palsy in the following patients based on their clinical features: Patient 1 - Deviation of angle of mouth to left, eyelids completely closed and wrinkling of the forehead. Patient 2 - Deviation of angle of mouth to left, the right eyelid remains partially open, and no wrinkling of the forehead.
options: A-Right LMN facial nerve palsy B-Left UMN facial nerve palsy
A-Right UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy
A-Left UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy
A-Left LMN facial nerve palsy B-Right UMN facial nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A-Left UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy

Patient 1 has left UMN facial nerve palsy, and patient 2 has right LMN facial nerve palsy.

In an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, wrinkling of the forehead and eyelid closure remain intact because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral cortical innervation. In this case, the right side of the face is affected, as evidenced by deviation of the angle of the mouth towards the left (normal) side - a key indicator of facial palsy, since the mouth always deviates towards the normal side due to loss of muscle tone on the affected side.

The first-order neurons originate from the left cerebral hemisphere, cross over to the right facial nerve nucleus in the pons, and synapse there. From this nucleus, second-order neurons of the right facial nerve descend to supply the right side of the face. Hence, a left UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the right side, while forehead movement is preserved.

In contrast, a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion affects both the upper and lower facial muscles on the same (ipsilateral) side, leading to loss of forehead wrinkling, incomplete eye closure, and drooping of the mouth. In this patient, since the mouth deviates towards the left, it indicates a right LMN facial nerve palsy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Molecular defect causing liver disease in Dubin-Johnson syndrome is__________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ABCC2

The molecular defect causing liver disease in Dubin–Johnson syndrome is ABCC2.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder due to a defect in ABCC2. ABCC2 codes for canalicular protein with ATP-binding cassette. A defect in this gene leads to the mutation of the multiple drug-resistant protein 2 (MRP2) receptor. This in turn leads to a defective transfer of conjugated bilirubin from the liver to bile.

It presents with abdominal pain, mild icterus, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Biopsy shows black liver due to an accumulation of epinephrine metabolite.

Conditions causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia are summarised in the table below:

Dubin-Johnson syndrome

The absent function of multiple drug-resistant proteins (MRP-2)
Defects in anion transport

No abnormal liver pigmentation.

Normal levels of coproporphyrin in urine
Increased levels of coproporphyrin in urine

The gall bladder is not visualized on oral cholecystography
The gall bladder is visualized on oral cholecystography

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries does not supply the corresponding region of the dura mater?
options: Middle meningeal artery – Anterior cranial fossa
Accessory meningeal branch of maxillary artery – Middle cranial fossa
Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – Posterior cranial fossa
Meningeal branch of anterior and posterior ethmoid artery – Anterior cranial fossa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – Posterior cranial fossa

The meningeal branch of the internal carotid artery (ICA) does not supply the posterior cranial fossa. It supplies the anterior cranial fossa.

The dura mater is supplied by meningeal arteries that pass along the inner periosteum (endosteum) of the skull over the endosteal layer of the dura and supply the following regions.

Region
Arteries

Anterior cranial fossa

• Meningeal branches of anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries
• Meningeal branches of internal carotid arteries
• A branch of the middle meningeal artery

Middle cranial fossa

• Middle meningeal artery and accessory meningeal branches of the maxillary artery
• A branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery
• Branches of the internal carotid artery
• A recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery

Posterior cranial fossa

• Meningeal branches of the occipital artery
• Posterior meningeal branches of the vertebral artery
• Dorsal meningeal and tentorial arteries arising from the meningohypophyseal trunk
questions.learning: Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – Posterior cranial fossa The meningeal branch of the internal carotid artery (ICA) does not supply the posterior cranial fossa.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old individual with a history of presbyopia suddenly finds they can read fine print, such as a newspaper, without using glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis explaining this change in vision?
questions.explanation: The phenomenon where an elderly patient suddenly regains the ability to read without glasses is colloquially known as "second sight." This is most commonly caused by nuclear sclerosis, a type of age-related cataract. As the lens nucleus becomes more dense and dehydrated, its refractive index increases. This "index myopia" shifts the patient's overall refraction toward nearsightedness. For a presbyopic patient who previously required plus-powered reading glasses, this new myopic shift compensates for their loss of accommodation, allowing them to focus on near objects again without assistance. Index hypermetropia (Option B) would worsen the ability to see near objects. "Regression of presbyopia" (Option C) is a misnomer, as the physiological hardening of the lens that causes presbyopia is irreversible; the change is refractive, not accommodative. While the improved near vision is a temporary convenience, it usually signals the progression of a cataract that will eventually blur distant vision significantly. Therefore, index myopia due to nuclear cataract is the correct clinical diagnosis for this specific visual change
questions.learning: The phenomenon where an elderly patient suddenly regains the ability to read without glasses is colloquially known as "second sight." This is most commonly caused by nuclear sclerosis, a type of age-related cataract.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old person with a history of intravenous drug abuse presents with malaise, fatigue, rigors, and a pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. Based on these clinical features and risk factors, which organism is most likely to be isolated on blood culture?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of infective endocarditis (IE), specifically right-sided involvement as indicated by the pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border (tricuspid regurgitation). Intravenous drug users (IVDU) have a high risk of developing IE, and Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism in this population, accounting for over 50% of cases. It typically results in an acute, destructive form of the disease. Streptococcus sanguis (Option A) is a common cause of subacute IE but is usually associated with dental procedures. Enterococcus (Option B) is often linked to genitourinary manipulations. Coxiella burnetii (Option C) is the cause of Q fever endocarditis, which is much rarer. Given the specific lifestyle risk factor and the acute presentation (rigors), Staphylococcus aureus is the statistically and clinically most probable pathogen
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of infective endocarditis (IE), specifically right-sided involvement as indicated by the pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border (tricuspid regurgitation).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the management of bacterial vaginosis (BV), certain antibiotics are not advised according to CDC guidelines. Which antibiotic is specifically not recommended for treating BV?
questions.explanation: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) results from a shift in vaginal flora where lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis. According to CDC guidelines, Erythromycin (Option D) is not recommended for the treatment of BV as it has poor activity against the causative organisms. The first-line recommended treatments include Metronidazole (Option A) (either oral or vaginal gel) and Clindamycin (Option C) (cream or oral). Tinidazole (Option B) is an alternative oral regimen recommended by the CDC. BV is diagnosed clinically using Amsel's criteria: thin white discharge, vaginal pH , positive "whiff" test, and "clue cells" on microscopy. Treatment is indicated for symptomatic women and all pregnant women to reduce the risk of preterm birth. Partners are generally not treated as it does not prevent recurrence. It is important to advise patients on Metronidazole to avoid alcohol to prevent a disulfiram-like reaction
questions.learning: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) results from a shift in vaginal flora where lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis. According to CDC guidelines, Erythromycin (Option D) is not recommended for the treatment of BV as it has poor activity…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a neurotransmitter derived from aminoacids ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatine

Creatine is not a neurotransmitter derived from amino acids.

Creatine is an intermediate product in the process of formation of creatinine. The steps involved in the formation are as follows:

• The amidino group of arginine is transferred to glycine to form guanidoacetic acid. This step occurs in the kidneys and pancreas.
• Guanido acetic acid is methylated by S-adenosyl methionine to form creatine. This step occurs in the liver.

Creatine is phosphorylated to creatine phosphate by the enzyme creatine kinase, which is present in the muscle, brain and liver. The reaction needs hydrolysis of ATP. The stored creatine phosphate in the muscle serves as an immediate store of energy in the muscle. During muscle contraction, the energy is first derived from ATP hydrolysis. Thereafter, the ATP is regenerated by the hydrolysis of creatine phosphate. This is called the Lohmann's reaction.

The creatine phosphate may be converted to its anhydride, creatinine, which is excreted in the urine. Creatinine level in the blood is an indicator of renal function.

Other options :

Option A - Gamma amino butyric acid (GABA) functions in brain tissue as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. It is formed by decarboxylation of glutamate by L-glutamate decarboxylase.

Option B - Dopa is a precursor in the formation of the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. It is formed by the hydroxylation of tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase.

Option C - 5 Hydroxytryptamine is an important neurotransmitter in the brain, where it functions as an antidepressant. It is derived from the amino acid tryptophan, in a process of hydroxylation followed by decarboxylation.
questions.learning: Creatine Creatine is not a neurotransmitter derived from amino acids. Creatine is an intermediate product in the process of formation of creatinine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to jaundice: 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL. 2. If the examiner suspects scleral icterus, second site to examine is underneath the tongue. 3. In long-standing jaundice, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin. 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to its high elastin content. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4 only

Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 2–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign because the sclera is rich in elastin, which has a high affinity for bilirubin. If scleral icterus is doubtful, the undersurface of the tongue (sublingual mucosa) should be examined, as it is another early site of bilirubin deposition.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL ✔️: Clinically, scleral icterus is usually evident when bilirubin is \~2–3 mg/dL.
• 2. If scleral icterus is suspected\, examine underneath the tongue ✔️: The sublingual mucosa is an early site for detecting jaundice.
• 3. In long-standing jaundice\, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin ❌: The green discoloration is due to oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin, not reduction.
• 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to high elastin content ✔️: Correct.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 only Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 2–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign because the sclera is rich in elastin, which has a high affinity for bilirubin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The marked structure serves as a surface landmark for which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus.

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere. It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insular cortex.

Pterion marks as a surface landmark for the following structures:

• Middle meningeal artery and vein: fractures in this area can rupture the middle meningeal artery, leading to an epidural hematoma.
• Broca’s area: Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) in the inferior frontal gyrus, it lies in proximity to the pterion
• The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to the pterion, beneath the lateral sulcus.
• Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery and its branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization.

During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull).

Other Options:

Option A: The pineal gland is located in the posterior aspect of the cranial fossa in the brain. It is located deep in the brain, near the midline.

Option B: Wenicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere. It is found in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus.

Option D: The internal carotid artery siphon is a part of the internal carotid artery's course. Characterized by its S-shaped curvature as it traverses the cavernous sinus and enters the cranial cavity. This configuration helps dissipate pulsatile energy, reducing stress on cerebral vessels, and allows adaptability to cranial movements while maintaining cerebral perfusion.
questions.learning: Stem of the lateral sulcus — The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus. The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which statement regarding the structure and composition of bone is incorrect?
options: Osteocytes are the major cell type in mature bone
Collagen is synthesized in bone osteoblasts
Calcium phosphate is one of the major inorganic minerals
questions.explanation: In bone histology and biochemistry, the organic matrix (osteoid) is primarily composed of Type 1 collagen fibers, not Type 2. Type 1 collagen provides the high tensile strength required for skeletal integrity. Type 2 collagen is characteristic of cartilage, not bone. Statement A is true; osteocytes, which are trapped osteoblasts within lacunae, are the most numerous and long-lived cells in mature bone. Statement B is true; osteoblasts are the cells responsible for the synthesis and secretion of the organic bone matrix, including collagen and non-collagenous proteins. Statement D is true; the inorganic component of bone consists mainly of hydroxyapatite crystals, which are a form of calcium phosphate, providing compressive strength. Understanding that bone is a Type 1 collagen-based tissue is critical for diagnosing conditions like Osteogenesis Imperfecta, which results from mutations in Type 1 collagen genes. Therefore, Option C is the only false statement among the provided choices regarding bone composition
questions.learning: In bone histology and biochemistry, the organic matrix (osteoid) is primarily composed of Type 1 collagen fibers, not Type 2. Type 1 collagen provides the high tensile strength required for skeletal integrity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 74-year-old man presents with low back pain radiating to the leg. Spinal examination reveals a palpable “step” in the lumbosacral region, as seen on the provided X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s clinical finding of a palpable "step-off" in the lumbosacral region is pathognomonic for Spondylolisthesis (Option B) . Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward translation or slipping of one vertebra over another. The provided X-ray confirms this, showing the L5 vertebral body clearly displaced anteriorly relative to the S1 segment. Spondylolysis (Option A) refers to a defect or stress fracture in the pars interarticularis but without the actual "slip" or step-off. Spondylosis (Option D) is a general term for age-related degenerative changes (osteoarthritis) of the spine. Disc prolapse (Option C) causes radiating pain but would not result in a structural bony step on palpation or lateral X-ray. Therefore, because of the definitive radiological visual of vertebral displacement and the corresponding physical exam finding, spondylolisthesis is the correct diagnosis. It is commonly associated with degenerative changes in older adults or prior lysis in younger patients
questions.learning: The patient’s clinical finding of a palpable "step-off" in the lumbosacral region is pathognomonic for Spondylolisthesis (Option B) . Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward translation or slipping of one vertebra over another.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic examination, a skull bone was brought by police whose cephalic index came out to be 85. Skull bone belongs to which race?
questions.explanation: The cephalic index (CI) is a key anthropometric measurement used in forensic science to determine ancestry by calculating the ratio of skull breadth to length. A cephalic index of 85 falls into the "brachycephalic" or short-headed category (defined as CI ). This range is characteristic of the Mongoloid race (East Asians). Regarding the other options, pure Aryans and African (Negroid) populations (Options B and (C) are typically "dolichocephalic" or long-headed, with a cephalic index below 75. Europeans (Caucasoids) and many Indian populations (Option D) often fall into the "mesaticephalic" or medium-headed category, with a CI between 75 and 79.9. Because 85 is significantly higher than these ranges, it points definitively toward Mongoloid ancestry. This objective measurement allows forensic experts to narrow down the possible identity of skeletal remains during a medicolegal investigation
questions.learning: The cephalic index (CI) is a key anthropometric measurement used in forensic science to determine ancestry by calculating the ratio of skull breadth to length.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with generalised edema and was found to have hypercholesterolemia. Urine analysis shows protein 3+ and fat bodies. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nephrotic syndrome

The clinical scenario showing a child with generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, massive proteinuria, and fat bodies in urine is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome.

Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by nephrotic range proteinuria/heavy proteinuria >3.5 g/24 hr or urine protein: creatinine ratio > 2 and is associated with a triad of hypoalbuminemia (≤2.5 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia (cholesterol > 200 mg/dL).

Nephrotic syndrome in children is primarily idiopathic, with minimal change disease being the most common glomerular lesion. Podocyte injury or genetic mutations in podocyte proteins can lead to nephrotic-range proteinuria.

Edema is the most common presenting symptom. They have elevated levels of cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoproteins (LDL), and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL). It is caused by both increased lipid synthesis and decreased lipid catabolism.

They are prone to infections especially by encapsulated bacteria due to factors such as urinary losses of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement factors (C3, C5, factors B and D). Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state due to vascular stasis, increased platelet, increased hepatic production of fibrinogen, and urinary losses of antithrombotic factors such as antithrombin III and protein S.

The diagnosis is confirmed by performing a urinalysis and urine protein: creatinine ratio. The recommended initial treatment for nephrotic syndrome is a daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) of prednisolone for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks.

Definitions regarding the course of nephrotic syndrome:

• Remission is characterized by a urine protein: creatinine ratio of <0.2 or <1+ protein on urine dipstick testing for 3 consecutive days
• Response in nephrotic syndrome is defined as achieving remission within the initial 4 weeks of corticosteroid therapy
• Relapse is indicated by an increase in urine protein: creatinine ratio >0.2 or a reading of 2+ and higher for 3 consecutive days.
• Frequently relapsing: ≥2 relapses in 6 months or 4 relapses in 12 months.
• Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome: Relapse during steroid tapering or within 2 weeks of discontinuation.
• Steroid resistance: Failure to achieve remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone for 4 weeks and alternate days for the next 4 weeks.

Other options :

Option B: Nephritic syndrome classically presents with tea- or cola-colored urine (hematuria), edema, hypertension, and oliguria.

Option C: Goodpasture disease is an autoimmune condition characterized by pulmonary hemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and elevated anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody levels.

Option D: IgA nephropathy is an immune complex-mediated disease, with a predominance of IgA within glomerular mesangial deposits. They present with gross hematuria and proteinuria.
questions.learning: Nephrotic syndrome — The clinical scenario showing a child with generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, massive proteinuria, and fat bodies in urine is highly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a known penicillin allergy presents with fever and burning micturition, along with hearing impairment and dizziness. Which drug would be the most appropriate choice for management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) and pre-existing hearing/balance issues. Given the penicillin allergy, beta-lactams like Ampicillin-Clavulanic acid (Option D) are contraindicated. Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, is highly effective against common Gram-negative uropathogens and is safe for penicillin-allergic patients. Regarding the other choices, Amikacin (Option B) is an aminoglycoside that provides excellent UTI coverage but is notoriously ototoxic and nephrotoxic; using it in a patient who already has hearing problems and dizziness would be dangerous. Azithromycin (Option A) is a macrolide that has poor urinary tract penetration and is not a first-line agent for UTI. Ciprofloxacin offers the best balance of efficacy for burning micturition while avoiding exacerbation of the patient’s otologic symptoms. Therefore, Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate and safest management choice in this specific clinical scenario
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) and pre-existing hearing/balance issues. Given the penicillin allergy, beta-lactams like Ampicillin-Clavulanic acid (Option D) are contraindicated.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the specific term used to describe this autopsy finding commonly observed in cases of drowning?
questions.explanation: The image shows a dead body’s hand tightly clutching weeds/grass, which is a classic finding in drowning cases. This phenomenon is known as cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor). Cadaveric spasm is a rare form of muscular stiffening that occurs immediately at the moment of death, without the usual relaxation phase seen before rigor mortis. It typically affects voluntary muscles, especially the hands, and preserves the last activity performed by the person before death. In drowning, the victim often struggles and grasps surrounding objects like weeds, mud, or grass, which remain firmly held due to cadaveric spasm. This is considered strong forensic evidence of antemortem drowning. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Cutis anserina: Goosebumps due to cold exposure, not gripping (C) Rigor mortis: Develops gradually after death, not instantaneous (D) Washerwoman’s hands: Skin wrinkling due to prolonged immersion
questions.learning: The image shows a dead body’s hand tightly clutching weeds/grass, which is a classic finding in drowning cases. This phenomenon is known as cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the contraindications for the use of ventouse (vacuum extraction) during delivery?
questions.explanation: Vacuum extraction (ventouse) is contraindicated in preterm infants, generally defined as less than 34 weeks of gestation. This is because the preterm fetal head is soft and the scalp is more fragile, significantly increasing the risk of intracranial hemorrhage and subgaleal hematoma from the suction pressure. Heart disease (Option B) and decreased bear-down efforts (Option A) are actually indications for instrumental delivery (forceps or vacuum) to shorten the second stage of labor and reduce maternal effort. Dilatation (Option D) is not a contraindication; however, for any instrumental delivery, the cervix must be fully dilated . If the cervix is not fully dilated, an instrumental attempt is contraindicated. Other contraindications for ventouse include fetal face presentation and suspected fetal bleeding disorders. Consequently, prematurity stands out as a major relative contraindication due to fetal vulnerability

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Diamox is given to a patient with glaucoma. It is a non-competitive inhibitor of the carbonic anhydrase enzyme. Which of the following would be the effect of this drug?
options: Decrease in both Km and Vmax
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decrease in Vmax

Non-competitive inhibitors cause a decrease in Vmax.

In non-competitive inhibition:

• The inhibitor binds to the adjacent site and not the catalytic site of the enzyme
• The catalytic property of the enzyme is reduced and hence Vmax is decreased
• The affinity of the enzyme is not altered and hence Km is unaltered

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young female presented with complaints of lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, history of IUCD use for last 3–4 years. On examination, the patient had fever, adnexal/cervical motion tenderness and increased ESR and C-reactive protein. What is the probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute PID

Acute Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum. The patient has the classical features:

• Lower abdominal pain
• Vaginal discharge
• Long-term IUCD use (risk factor)
• Fever
• Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness
• Raised ESR and CRP indicating inflammation

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Ectopic pregnancy: Usually presents with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy should always be excluded with a β-hCG test, but vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness with inflammatory markers favor PID.
• B. Acute appendicitis: Typically causes right iliac fossa pain, anorexia, nausea, and localized peritoneal signs without vaginal discharge or cervical motion tenderness.
• C. Diverticulitis: Usually occurs in older patients, presenting with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and bowel symptoms rather than gynecological findings.
questions.learning: Acute PID Acute Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male with history of alcohol use presents with high-grade fever and right upper quadrant pain for 6 days. Ultrasound shows a solitary hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe 5cm. Aspiration produces sterile brown, semi-liquid material. His serology for E. histolytica is negative at admission. What is the best next step?
options: Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + repeat imaging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start metronidazole therapy

This patient has features that are highly suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess (ALA) despite a negative serology at admission.

Clues favoring amoebic liver abscess

• Middle-aged male with alcohol use (strong risk factor)
• High-grade fever + right upper quadrant pain
• Solitary abscess in the right lobe (5 cm)
• Aspiration yields sterile brown, semi-liquid material ("anchovy sauce" pus), which is characteristic of amoebic liver abscess
• Culture-negative aspirate supports ALA rather than pyogenic liver abscess

Why is the serology negative?

The patient has had symptoms for only 6 days.

• Antibodies to Entamoeba histolytica usually become detectable after 7–10 days of illness.
• Therefore, early serology may be falsely negative.
• A negative serology does not exclude amoebic liver abscess during the first week.

Why is metronidazole the best next step?

The clinical picture is almost diagnostic of amoebic liver abscess, and treatment should not be delayed waiting for repeat serology.

Treatment

• Metronidazole (or tinidazole)
• Followed by a luminal amoebicide (e.g., diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) to eradicate intestinal cysts.

Why are the other options incorrect?

A. Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + repeat imaging ❌

• Appropriate for pyogenic liver abscess, which usually presents with:

• Multiple abscesses
• Purulent aspirate
• Positive bacterial cultures

• Here, the aspirate is sterile brown ("anchovy sauce"), favoring amoebic abscess.

C. Repeat USG-guided aspiration ❌

• Aspiration is not routinely required for amoebic liver abscess.
• Indications include:

• Left lobe abscess
• Large abscess (>5 cm with impending rupture)
• No improvement after 48–72 hours of metronidazole
• Diagnostic uncertainty

The aspiration has already established the characteristic appearance.

D. Plan for surgical drainage ❌

Reserved for:

• Ruptured abscess
• Failure of percutaneous drainage
• Complicated abscesses

Not indicated initially.

High-yield points for exam (ZVrecommended!):

| Feature | Amoebic liver abscess | Pyogenic liver abscess

| ------- | --------------------- | ----------------------

| Number | Usually solitary | Often multiple

| Location | Right lobe | Variable

| Aspirate | Sterile, brown "anchovy sauce" | Thick yellow pus

| Culture | Usually sterile | Positive bacterial culture

| Serology | Positive in >90% after 7–10 days | Negative

| Treatment | Metronidazole + luminal agent | Broad-spectrum antibiotics ± drainage
questions.learning: Start metronidazole therapy — This patient has features that are highly suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess (ALA) despite a negative serology at admission.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The audiogram given in the image below is seen in ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endolymphatic hydrops

The given image shows an upsloping/ ascending audiogram in which lower frequencies are affected first like in the early stages of Meniere's disease also known as endolymphatic hydrops.

Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) is an inner ear disorder where the endolymph distends the endolymphatic system.

Meniere's disease is usually unilateral. It is characterized by episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of ear fullness.

Pure tone audiometry reveals a sensorineural type of hearing loss with lower frequencies affected first. It shows a rising type of curve. As the disease progresses, middle and higher frequencies get involved, and the audiogram becomes flat or downsloping type.

The illustration given below shows an audiogram seen in different stages of Meniere's disease.

Other options:

Option A: Ototoxicity causes bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Audiometry shows a downsloping audiogram, typically involving frequencies above 8,000 Hz and progresses to lower speech frequencies. Common drugs causing the same include aminoglycoside antibiotics; loop diuretics (not thiazides); antimalarials; cisplatin; and NSAIDs like ibuprofen, salicylates, and indomethacin.

Option B: Presbycusis is a physiological sensorineural hearing loss occurring in individuals above 65 years of age. Audiometry shows a downsloping graph.

Option C: In noise-induced hearing loss, audiometry shows a typical notch at 4000 Hz. As the duration of noise exposure increases, the notch becomes deeper and wider, involving lower and higher frequencies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Breast cancer of size 6 x 8 cm with dimpling with invasion of Pectoralis Major and ipsilateral matted axillary nodes belongs to what TNM stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. T3N2M0

Tumor size = 6 × 8 cm

Largest dimension = 8 cm

So tumor is:

• 5 cm → T3

Dimpling of skin

Skin dimpling/tethering alone does not make it T4.

T4 requires:

• Ulceration
• Satellite skin nodules
• Peau d’orange
• Chest wall invasion

Invasion of Pectoralis Major

Invasion of pectoralis major muscle alone is NOT chest wall invasion.

Chest wall invasion (T4a) means invasion of:

• Ribs
• Intercostal muscles
• Serratus anterior

NOT pectoralis muscle.

Hence still T3, not T4.

Ipsilateral matted axillary lymph nodes

Matted/fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes = N2

No distant metastasis mentioned

→ M0

Final TNM Stage

| Component | Stage

| --------- | -----

| Tumor >5 cm | T3

| Matted axillary nodes | N2

| No metastasis | M0

Final Answer: T3N2M0

| T1 | Tumour ≤ 20 mm in greatest dimension

| T1mi | Tumour ≤ 1 mm

| T1a | Tumour > 1 mm but ≤ 5 mm (round 1.0–1.9 mm to 2 mm)

| T1b | Tumour > 5 mm but ≤ 10 mm

| T1c | Tumour > 10 mm but ≤ 20 mm

| T2 | Tumour > 20 mm but ≤ 50 mm

| T3 | Tumour > 50 mm

| T4 | Tumour of any size with extension to chest wall and/or skin (dermis alone not included)

| T4a | Extension to chest wall (pectoral muscle involvement alone does not qualify)

| T4b | Skin ulceration, satellite nodules, or oedema (peau d’orange), not inflammatory carcinoma

| T4c | Both T4a and T4b present

| T4d | Inflammatory carcinoma (peau d’orange, redness > 1/3rd breast ± lump)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A randomized trial comparing the efficacy of two drugs showed a difference between the two with a p value of <0.005. In reality, both drugs do not differ at all. This is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha error

• In this scenario, let’s take the null hypothesis as the two drugs being the same, which the questions states, is true in reality.
• The alternative hypothesis will then be that both drugs are different.
• The questions states that p value was found to be < 0.005, which is statistically significant and so the null hypothesis is rejected.
• But we already know that the null hypothesis is true and we are forced to accept the alternative hypothesis even though it is false.
• This is a type I error or alpha error.
• When an alternative hypothesis is accepted even when it is false and the null hypothesis is true, it is a type I error or false positive error.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the affinity of carbon monoxide to hemoglobin in comparison to oxygen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 250

CO binds to hemoglobin with an affinity that is 250 times that of O2 to form carboxyhemoglobin.

CO also increases the O2 affinity of remaining free hemoglobin sites (causes left shift of the O2 - hemoglobin dissociation curve).

* Curve A - Myoglobin O2-dissociation curve

* Curve B - Normal Hb O2-dissociation curve

* Curve C- CO binds to hemoglobin and prevents O2 binding

* Curve D - Anemia

Carbon monoxide (CO) reacts with hemoglobin to form carbon monoxyhemoglobin (carboxyhemoglobin or COHb). The affinity of hemoglobin for CO is 210 times its affinity for O2, and COHb liberates CO very slowly. An additional difficulty is that when COHb is present, the dissociation curve of the remaining HbO2 shifts to the left, decreasing the amount of O2 released.

Treatment of CO poisoning consists of ventilation with oxygen since oxygen hastens the dissociation of carboxyhemoglobin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a famous large prospective study that helped establish risk factors for coronary heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Framingham study

The Framingham Heart Study (FHS) is the landmark prospective cohort study that identified the major modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD) and laid the foundation for modern cardiovascular prevention.

• A. Adelaide study ✗

• Not a landmark study for CHD risk factors.

• B. Birmingham study ✗

• Not associated with establishing CHD risk factors.

• C. Framingham study ✓

• Began in 1948 in Framingham, Massachusetts, USA.
• Followed thousands of participants over decades to identify risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

• D. Pittsburg study ✗

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following tissues is unable to take up glucose in the absence of insulin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Skeletal muscles

Glucose uptake in different tissues depends on specific glucose transporters (GLUTs), some of which are insulin dependent.

• Skeletal muscle and adipose tissue require insulin for glucose entry.
• Insulin stimulates translocation of GLUT-4 transporters to the cell membrane.
• Without insulin, GLUT-4 does not move to the membrane, so glucose uptake is markedly reduced.

Therefore, skeletal muscle cannot effectively take up glucose in the absence of insulin.

Some tissues use transporters that do not require insulin:

• RBCs → GLUT-1
• Brain → GLUT-1 and GLUT-3
• Kidney, liver, pancreatic β-cells → GLUT-2

These tissues can take up glucose even during fasting or insulin deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids are necessary for purine ring formation?
questions.explanation: The purine ring (the core of adenine and guanine) is constructed atom-by-atom on a ribose-5-phosphate scaffold. Three specific amino acids contribute various nitrogen and carbon atoms to this structure: Glycine, Aspartate, and Glutamine. Glycine contributes the C4, C5, and N7 atoms. Glutamine provides the amide nitrogen for N3 and N9. Aspartate contributes the amino nitrogen for N1. Other contributors (not listed) include and N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate. Valine (Option A) and Glutamate (Option C) are not directly incorporated into the purine ring. Asparagine (Option D) is not a purine precursor. This pathway is clinically targeted by many drugs: methotrexate inhibits folate contribution, while 6-mercaptopurine and mycophenolate mofetil interfere with purine synthesis to treat cancers and autoimmune diseases. Understanding the raw materials required for nucleotide synthesis is a classic high-yield biochemistry topic, linking nutrition and metabolism directly to the body's ability to replicate DNA and produce energy-carrying molecules like ATP
questions.learning: The purine ring (the core of adenine and guanine) is constructed atom-by-atom on a ribose-5-phosphate scaffold. Three specific amino acids contribute various nitrogen and carbon atoms to this structure: Glycine, Aspartate, and Glutamine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common non-pancreatic site for tumour distribution in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duodenum

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma). The most common site overall is the duodenum, followed by the pancreas. Thus, the most common non-pancreatic site is the duodenum.

Why not the other options?

• B. Ovaries: Extremely rare site for gastrinoma.
• C. Stomach: Gastrinomas do not commonly arise in the stomach.
• D. Liver: The liver is the most common site of metastasis, not the primary tumor.
questions.learning: Duodenum Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma). The most common site overall is the duodenum, followed by the pancreas.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient was treated with TCA for a major depressive episode in the hospital for 4 weeks. What is the main concern while considering his discharge from the hospital?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Suicidal risk

Suicidal thoughts or behavior are a side effect of TCAs. Therefore, the attendants of the patient should be warned regarding this when a patient gets discharged after being treated with TCAs for a major depressive episode.

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are drugs that act by inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin from the synaptic clefts.

The side effects of TCAs are due to blockade of other receptors:

• Muscarinic M receptors- constipation, dry mouth, arrhythmia
• Histamine H1 receptors- sedation
• 5HT receptors - weight gain due to increased appetite
• Alpha1 receptors - postural hypotension.

The various classes of drugs used in depression and anxiety are listed below:

Class of drugs
Examples

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents to the pediatric emergency department with a 5-day history of low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and a characteristic barking cough. On examination, he has a hoarse voice, moderate pharyngeal congestion, and mild tachypnea. A chest X-ray shows subglottic narrowing with the classic steeple sign, consistent with croup. In this clinical scenario, which of the following treatment options is not recommended?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and the radiographic "steeple sign" are diagnostic of Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis), which is a viral respiratory infection most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus. Because the etiology is viral, parenteral antibiotics like cefotaxime (Option B) are NOT recommended and have no role in standard croup management unless a secondary bacterial infection is suspected. Standard treatments include nebulized racemic epinephrine (Option A) for rapid reduction of mucosal edema and intramuscular or oral dexamethasone (Option D) to provide longer-lasting anti-inflammatory effects. Heliox (Option C) can be used in severe cases to reduce turbulent airflow and the work of breathing. In contrast, bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis would require antibiotics, but the "barking cough" and "steeple sign" specifically confirm croup. Therefore, unnecessary antibiotics are the incorrect choice in this setting
questions.learning: The clinical presentation and the radiographic "steeple sign" are diagnostic of Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis), which is a viral respiratory infection most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia says, “Lord Hanuman was celibate, I am celibate, so I am Lord Hanuman.” Which thought abnormality is present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autistic Thinking

This is autistic thinking, where illogical reasoning equates two entities based on one shared property (Von Domarus law). Verbigeration is purposeless repetition, neologism is new words, and loosening of association is unrelated sentence flow.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 4-day history of high-grade fever and sore throat. His parents report that he has difficulty swallowing, drools continuously, and refuses to eat. They also noticed that he keeps his neck flexed and cries whenever they try to extend it. On examination, the child has a muffled ("hot potato") voice, torticollis, and a bulge over the posterior pharyngeal wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retropharyngeal abscess

• Retropharyngeal abscess causes widening of the prevertebral soft tissue on lateral neck X-ray.
• Common in children under 5 years due to retropharyngeal lymph nodes.
• Presents with fever, drooling, neck stiffness, dysphagia, and torticollis.
• Airway compromise is an important complication.
• CT neck with contrast confirms the diagnosis.
• Treatment includes IV antibiotics and drainage if indicated.

Other options:

• A. Peritonsillar abscess produces uvular deviation rather than prevertebral widening.
• B. Ludwig angina involves the submandibular space.
• C. Parapharyngeal abscess is lateral to the pharynx.
• Normal prevertebral soft tissue at C2 <7 mm (adults) and <14 mm (children).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the LOX pathway shown, drug ‘X’ selectively blocks the receptor for cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4), thereby preventing bronchoconstriction. Identify drug ‘X’.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Montelukast

Montelukast is a selective cysteinyl leukotriene (CysLT₁) receptor antagonist that blocks the actions of LTC₄, LTD₄, and LTE₄, thereby preventing bronchoconstriction, airway edema, and mucus secretion. It is used for the prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma, especially aspirin-induced asthma and exercise-induced bronchospasm, as well as allergic rhinitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Zileuton: Inhibits 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), thereby preventing the synthesis of all leukotrienes (LTB₄, LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄). It does not block the leukotriene receptor.
• C. Indomethacin: A non-selective COX inhibitor that inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and has no direct effect on leukotriene receptors.
• D. Prednisolone: Inhibits phospholipase A₂ (via lipocortin induction), reducing the formation of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes upstream, but does not selectively block cysteinyl leukotriene receptors.
questions.learning: Montelukast Montelukast is a selective cysteinyl leukotriene (CysLT₁) receptor antagonist that blocks the actions of LTC₄, LTD₄, and LTE₄, thereby preventing bronchoconstriction, airway edema, and mucus secretion.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with muscle weakness, diarrhea, and bradycardia and is diagnosed with organophosphate poisoning. Atropine is administered as part of the treatment. Which of the following effects would not be observed after atropine administration?
questions.explanation: Organophosphate (OP) poisoning causes cholinergic overstimulation by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist specifically used to reverse muscarinic symptoms such as bradycardia, bronchorrhea, and diarrhea. Therefore, bradycardia is "not seen" after successful atropinization; the goal of treatment is to increase the heart rate to above 80 beats/minute. Muscle weakness (Option B) is a nicotinic effect at the neuromuscular junction and is not reversed by atropine, so it remains present until oximes (like pralidoxime) are given. Diaphoresis (Option C) and nasal discharge (Option D) are muscarinic effects that were present initially but should improve or resolve after atropine administration. Successful treatment is clinically monitored by looking for signs of "atropinization," including dry axillae, clear breath sounds on auscultation, and dilated pupils
questions.learning: Organophosphate (OP) poisoning causes cholinergic overstimulation by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Mechanism of action of Oseltamivir as an antiviral agent is:
options: Inhibition of RNA dependent DNA polymerase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neuraminidase inhibition

Oseltamivir and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors.

They competitively and reversibly interact with the enzyme sites to inhibit viral neuraminidase activity. This interferes with the release of the progeny from infected host cells, halting the spread of infection. Early administration is crucial.

Oseltamivir is given at a dose of 75 mg, twice a day for 5 days for the treatment of Influenza A and B. For prophylaxis, it is given at a dose of 75mg, once per day and continued for the duration of exposure.
questions.learning: Neuraminidase inhibition Oseltamivir and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors. They competitively and reversibly interact with the enzyme sites to inhibit viral neuraminidase activity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which step is not included in active management of third stage of labor (AMTSL)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bimanual compression

AMTSL consists of three main steps-

| Step | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Administration of uterotonics | Oxytocin given immediately after delivery

| Controlled cord traction | Brandt–Andrews maneuver

| Delayed cord clamping | Usually 1–3 minutes after birth

The third stage of labour is the period from delivery of the baby to expulsion of the placenta. Proper management is crucial to prevent Postpartum Hemorrhage, the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

1. Administration of Oxytocic

Oxytocin (10 IU IM/IV) is given immediately after delivery.

• Stimulates uterine contraction
• Compresses uterine blood vessels
• Prevents postpartum hemorrhage

Oxytocin is the drug of choice for prevention of PPH.

2. Brandt–Andrews Maneuver (Controlled Cord Traction)

This technique helps deliver the placenta safely.

Steps:

• One hand supports the uterus suprapubically
• The other hand applies traction on the umbilical cord

This prevents uterine inversion.

3. Delayed Cord Clamping

Delayed cord clamping means clamping the cord after 1–3 minutes.

Benefits:

• Improves neonatal hemoglobin levels
• Increases iron stores
• Reduces anemia in infancy

Bimanual Compression

Bimanual compression is not part of routine AMTSL.

It is used in management of postpartum hemorrhage, particularly when:

• Uterine atony occurs
• Bleeding persists despite uterotonics

Thus it is a treatment step, not a preventive step.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A contact lens user presents with the following clinical picture. He had watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant papillary conjunctivitis

The clinical history of watering, redness, foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles.

The patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae.

Papillae are reddish, flat-topped raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva These are the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium.

The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva.

Treatment includes removing the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine which have combined antihistamine and mast cell stabilizing effects are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases.

Other options:

Option A - Trachoma is caused by chlamydia trachomatis. In acute trachoma, sago grain follicles are characteristically seen as shown below.

Option B - Follicular conjunctivitis has follicles which are greyish-white raised areas seen on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. The image is shown below.

Option D - In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell–Lyon sign are present. Horner-Tranta’s spots which are discrete whitish raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer.

Image showing Horner-Tranta’s spots.

Pearl PF1374: WHO Programme to Control Trachoma: SAFE Strategy

* S—Surgery: Trichiasis and entropion correction surgery → 3° prevention.

* A—Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin, topical 1% tetracycline, topical 1% azithromycin → 2° prevention

* F—Facial hygiene → 1° prevention.

* E—Environmental cleanliness → primordial prevention

Strategy depends on the prevalence of trachoma follicle in children (1–9 yrs)

* Prevalence >10% → SAFE

* 5 to 10% → FE

* < 5% → NO intervention
questions.learning: Giant papillary conjunctivitis — The clinical history of watering, redness, foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs is associated with visual adverse effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ethambutol

Ethambutol is associated with ophthalmic toxicity.

Ethambutol inhibits arabinose transferase III, thereby decreasing arabinogalactan biosynthesis. This results in, disruption in mycobacterial cell wall synthesis. It is primarily excreted unchanged by kidneys and accumulation occurs in renal failure. Ethambutol does not undergo hepatic metabolism and can be safely prescribed for the treatment of TB in patients with hepatitis.

Optic neuritis resulting in decreased visual acuity and loss of ability to differentiate red from green is the most serious adverse effect of ethambutol. It is a dose-dependent adverse effect that can be unilateral or bilateral.

Tests of visual acuity and red-green discrimination before the start of therapy and periodically thereafter are recommended.

Pearl PF0763: Key points on the first line drugs used in the treatment of TB

Drugs
Isoniazid
Rifamycins
Pyrazinamide
Ethambutol

Mechanism of action
Blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
Inhibition of RNA polymerase, leading to the inhibition of RNA synthesis.
Inhibition of fatty acid synthase-I, leading to the inhibition of the cell membrane.
Inhibition of arabinosyl transferase, leading to a reduction in arabinogalactan needed for the cell wall.

Unique side effects

Shoulder hand syndrome and CNS side effects.

Orange urine, sweat, and tears. Flu-like symptoms with intermittent dosing.

The most hepatotoxic drug. It also causes hyperuricemia.

Optic neuritis and hence, not preferred in children.

Mechanism of resistance

Kat G mutation- the most severe form of resistance.

Inh a gene overexpression-  confers cross-resistance with ethionamide.

Mutation in rpoB- the gene coding for the β subunit of RNA polymerase.

Mutation of the Pnca gene.

Mutations in the embB gene.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with telecanthus, hypertelorism, an antimongoloid slant of the eyes, and associated congenital cardiac defects. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The child’s clinical features—telecanthus (increased distance between inner canthi), hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects—are highly characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (or Velocardiofacial syndrome). This condition is caused by a chromosomal microdeletion at the 22q11.2 locus. Regarding the distractors, translocations (Option A) involve the rearrangement of parts between non-homologous chromosomes and are common in leukemias. Inversions (Option B) are structural rearrangements within a single chromosome. Trisomy (Option D), such as Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), presents with a mongoloid (upward) slant rather than an antimongoloid one. Because the described cluster of facial and cardiac anomalies is the classic phenotype for the 22q11.2 deletion, a microdeletion is the correct genetic mechanism
questions.learning: The child’s clinical features—telecanthus (increased distance between inner canthi), hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes), antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects—are highly characteristic of DiGeorge syndrome (or Velocardiofacial syndrome).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A severely fatigued patient with markedly reduced responsiveness is brought to the emergency department. He has had a progressive loss of muscle strength over the past two days. A CT scan is performed, and the image is shown below. Which blood vessel is most likely occluded by a thrombus?
questions.explanation: The CT scan reveals a large area of hypodensity (darkness) involving the cortical and subcortical regions of the right cerebral hemisphere. This distribution is characteristic of an ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). The MCA is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery and supplies the majority of the lateral surface of the brain, including the motor and sensory areas for the face and upper limbs. A blood clot (thrombus or embolus) in the MCA results in dense contralateral hemiplegia and sensory loss. The anterior cerebral artery (Option B) supplies the medial surface (lower limbs), and the posterior cerebral artery (Option A) supplies the occipital lobe (vision). The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (Option D) supplies the cerebellum and lateral medulla. Given the widespread hemispheric involvement, the middle cerebral artery is the vessel occluded
questions.learning: The CT scan reveals a large area of hypodensity (darkness) involving the cortical and subcortical regions of the right cerebral hemisphere. This distribution is characteristic of an ischemic stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which among the following is the key feature of depression?
options: Loss of interest in pleasurable activties
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of interest in pleasurable activties

The key feature of depression among the given is loss of interest in pleasurable activities.

The Diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows:

A. Five or more of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period. At least one of the symptoms is either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure.

* Depressed mood most of the day

* Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)

* Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain, decrease or increase in appetite

* Insomnia or hypersomnia

* Psychomotor agitation or retardation

* Fatigue or loss of energy

* Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt

* Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness

* Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation

B. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition.

D. The occurrence of the major depressive episode is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders.

E. There has never been a manic episode or a hypomanic episode.
questions.learning: Loss of interest in pleasurable activties — The key feature of depression among the given is loss of interest in pleasurable activities. The Diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows: A.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman, a senior executive with a sedentary lifestyle, presents with palmoplantar pigmentation. X-ray of the spine shows calcification of intervertebral discs. Her urine gives a greenish-brown precipitate with Benedict's reagent and tests positive for reducing substances. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely in this patient?
options: (Option A is not printed in the source book)
questions.explanation: Homogentisic acid oxidase This clinical picture is characteristic of Alkaptonuria (Ochronosis). Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisic acid oxidase. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of homogentisic acid (HGA) in the blood and its subsequent excretion in the urine. HGA oxidizes and binds to connective tissues, causing dark pigmentation (ochronosis) in areas like the palms, soles, and sclera, as well as premature calcification of the intervertebral discs. Benedict’s reagent (typically used for glucose) can react with HGA to give a greenish-brown or orange-brown precipitate. Phenylalanine hydroxylase (Option A) deficiency causes phenylketonuria. Tyrosine hydroxylase (Option B) is involved in catecholamine synthesis. PHPP dioxygenase (Option D) is involved in tyrosine breakdown upstream of HGA oxidase. A classic sign of this condition is urine that turns black upon standing or when exposed to air (alkalization).
questions.learning: Homogentisic acid oxidase — This clinical picture is characteristic of Alkaptonuria (Ochronosis). Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisic acid oxidase.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Based on the MRI image, which structure is indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Body

The corpus callosum is the largest commissural white matter tract, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres. It is divided into four parts:

• Rostrum: Thin anterior-inferior portion
• Genu: Anterior bend
• Body (Trunk): Long central portion
• Splenium: Thickened posterior end

In this sagittal MRI, the arrow points to the central elongated segment, corresponding to the body of the corpus callosum.

Why not the other options?

• Rostrum: Thin, anterior-inferior part extending below the genu.
• Splenium: Thickened posterior end of the corpus callosum.
• Genu: Anterior curved portion forming the bend of the corpus callosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the following fracture.
options: Surgical neck humerus fracture with axillary nerve injury
Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy

The image shows a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus in which the radial nerve is commonly damaged.

Holstein and Lewis associated a special type of fracture of the distal humerus, a simple displaced spiral fracture, with the distal end deviating toward the radial side occurring in about 7% of all humeral shaft fractures, with an increased rate of radial nerve palsy.

Injuries of ulnar and median nerves associated with humeral shaft fractures are not as frequent as injuries of the radial nerve.

It clinically manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop).

Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Most cases of humerus shaft fractures can be managed conservatively using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing. Surgery is indicated in cases of open fractures, pathological fractures, simultaneous unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow), and in radial nerve palsy.  Surgical fixation can be performed by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins or an external fixator.
questions.learning: Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy — The image shows a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus in which the radial nerve is commonly damaged.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While checking the immunization technique of an ANM worker, you observe that she has used cotton, a syringe, and a needle. After immunization, which of the following statements regarding biomedical waste disposal is correct?
options: Syringe with needle in black translucent container
Used vial in translucent white container
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cotton swab in yellow bag

Under Biomedical Waste Management Rules, cotton swabs contaminated with blood or body fluids are classified as soiled waste.

Soiled waste is disposed of in the yellow bag, which is meant for incineration or deep burial.

Sharps (needles) go in white translucent puncture-proof containers, glass vials in blue, and syringes (without needles) in red, making option C correct.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presents to the hospital with fever and arthritis. Echocardiography confirms that this patient has carditis. He has a previous history of peptic ulcer disease. Which of the following anti-inflammatory drugs would be most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Celecoxib

The most appropriate anti-inflammatory drug for this patient is celecoxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor.

Several highly selective COX-2 inhibitors are used because of the potential benefit of blocking COX-2, which is produced at the sites of inflammation, without influencing the "housekeeping" COX-1 function. Compared to conventional NSAIDs, they reduce the risk of peptic ulcers and ulcer bleeding and cause less harm to the stomach mucosa. They do not inhibit platelet aggregation or prolong bleeding time, but they do decrease the vascular endothelium's production of PGI2.

Selective COX-2 inhibitors are less likely to cause gastric ulcers. Selective COX-2 inhibitors have analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects similar to those of non-selective NSAIDs but with better gastrointestinal tolerability.

The following drugs are preferential COX-2 inhibitors:

* Diclofenac

* Nimesulide

* Aceclofenac

* Etodolac

* Meloxicam

The following are selective COX-2 inhibitors:

* Celecoxib

* Etoricoxib

* Parecoxib

Since celecoxib confers a risk of cardiovascular hazard(myocardial infarction), physicians should use the lowest possible dose for the shortest possible duration.

Ibuprofen, aspirin, and flurbiprofen are nonselective COX inhibitors.

Naloxone is a competitive opiate antagonist that competes with opioids at their receptor sites.

The appropriate answer is high-dose aspirin or a corticosteroid like prednisone, depending on the severity of the carditis. The rationale for choosing celecoxib is its lower risk of gastrointestinal bleeding (compared to ibuprofen and diclofenac), which is slightly more favourable than the guaranteed high risk of bleeding from the other NSAIDs.

Pearl PF0755: Pure opioid antagonists

Naloxone: A short-acting opioid antagonist with a duration of action of 1-2 hours. Used in opioid overdose and respiratory depression in newborn due to perinatal opioid use.

Naltrexone: A Long-acting opioid antagonist with a with effects lasting till 48 hours. Used for prevention of relapse in opioid addiction treatment. It is associated with hepatotoxicity. It does not suppress craving in opioid addiction but suppresses craving in chronic alcoholics.

Nalmefene: A Long-acting opioid antagonist with a half-life of 8-10 hours administered intravenously. Used in opioid overdose like naloxone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The hormone acting on post ovulatory endometrium is: (NEET PG 2019)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Progesterone

Post ovulation, there is a significant rise in progesterone levels, which is crucial for the transformation of the endometrium into a secretory phase. This phase is essential for preparing the endometrium for potential implantation of an embryo.

Phases of the Menstrual Cycle:

1. Menstruation (0 - 4 days):

• The shedding of the endometrial lining occurs if there is no pregnancy.

2. Follicular Phase (10 - 14 days):

• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates the growth of ovarian follicles.
• Estrogen levels rise, leading to the proliferation of the endometrium.

3. Ovulation (14th day):

• Luteinizing hormone (LH) surge leads to the release of an ovum from the dominant follicle.

4. Luteal Phase (14 - 28 days):

• The corpus luteum forms and secretes progesterone.
• Progesterone causes the endometrium to develop secretory glands and prepare for implantation.
