questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents in early pregnancy with occasional spotting. The diagnosis of missed abortion is made when?
options: No cardiac activity at a CRL > 7mm
No cardiac activity at a CRL < 7mm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. No cardiac activity at a CRL > 7mm

Missed abortion is diagnosed when no cardiac activity is seen at a CRL greater than 7 mm.

In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, a gestational sac is visible on TVS by 4.5-5 weeks of LMP, the yolk sac appears at around 5.5 weeks, and by 6 weeks an embryo can be seen adjacent to the yolk sac. Cardiac activity of the embryo is usually detected on TVS at about 6–6.5 weeks.

A mean gestational sac diameter of ≥25 mm and a CRL of ≥7 mm are considered critical cut-off values, beyond which the absence of the expected structures is regarded as abnormal. Hence, missed abortion should be suspected if, on USG

* CRL ≥7 mm, and no cardiac activity is recorded (CRL-crown rump length)

* MSD ≥25 mm, and no embryo is seen (MSD-mean sac diameter)

Medical management can be performed with prostaglandin E1(misoprostol) or oxytocin. Surgical management in the form of dilatation and curettage can be performed.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heavy metal chelators are all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oxime

Heavy metal chelators are agents that bind toxic metals and form stable complexes that can be excreted from the body, thereby reducing metal toxicity.

Examples include:

• Penicillamine – used in copper poisoning and Wilson disease.
• BAL (Dimercaprol) – used in arsenic, mercury, and gold poisoning.
• Trientine – another copper chelator used in Wilson disease.

Oximes (e.g., pralidoxime) are not heavy-metal chelators. They are used in organophosphate poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the inhibited enzyme.
questions.learning: Oxime Heavy metal chelators are agents that bind toxic metals and form stable complexes that can be excreted from the body, thereby reducing metal toxicity.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which clinical test is being shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Cottle's test, which is used to evaluate the patency of the nasal valve. It involves pulling the patient's cheek laterally while they breathe in through the nose. If the nasal airway improves significantly upon pulling the cheek, the test is positive, indicating nasal valve collapse as a cause of obstruction. Epley's maneuver (Option A) is used to treat Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The Heimlich maneuver (Option B) is used to clear an obstructed airway. Trotter's method (Option D) is a posture used to control epistaxis (leaning forward and pinching the nose). Cottle's test is a simple, non-invasive diagnostic maneuver that helps surgeons determine if a patient with nasal obstruction requires specific correction of the internal nasal valve. Therefore, the visual of lateral cheek traction during respiration uniquely identifies this clinical test
questions.learning: The image depicts Cottle's test, which is used to evaluate the patency of the nasal valve. It involves pulling the patient's cheek laterally while they breathe in through the nose.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient, during his routine annual checkup, is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 40 mm in diameter on USG. Which of the following is true about the management of this patient?
options: Surgery is indicated if aneurysmal diameter is >55mm
Urgently wheel the patient to OT for surgery
Surgery is indicated only if aneurysm is >77mm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surgery is indicated if aneurysmal diameter is >55mm

Surgery is indicated in an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) only if its diameter is more than 55 mm in a male patient.

If the diameter is less than 55 mm, regular ultrasound monitoring is required. This is because elective open surgery has a higher rate of mortality when compared to conservative management for aneurysms of size < 55 mm.

Indications for surgery in abdominal aortic aneurysm:

• Size >5.5 cm in males
• Size >5 cm in females
• Expansion of >1 cm in one year
• Painful tender aneurysm
• Thrombosed aneurysm; aneurysm with distal emboli

Management of aortic aneurysm: AAA is surgically managed by dacron graft repair. It can be either open or EVAR (endovascular aneurysm repair)

• Open surgical repair is done by exposing the aorta through a mid-sternal incision and graft replacement. To expose the aorta the descending colon should be mobilized medially and this is known as left visceral rotation or Mattox procedure.
• EVAR is a minimally invasive procedure in which an aortic stent graft is placed on the nonaneurysmal aortoiliac segment.

Complications following an AAA repair are:

• Cardiovascular (ischemia and infarction)
• Respiratory (atelectasis or consolidation).
• Colonic ischemia.
• Renal failure.
• Aortoduodenal fistula
• spinal cord ischemia

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the type of placenta previa shown in the image below:
questions.explanation: In the given image, the placenta is located in the lower uterine segment and is seen reaching the edge of the internal cervical os but not covering it. This is the defining feature of marginal placenta previa. In marginal placenta previa, the placenta lies adjacent to the cervical opening (internal os) but does not overlap it. This distinguishes it from more severe types like partial or complete previa. Clinically, it may cause antepartum bleeding, but vaginal delivery may still be possible depending on the situation. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Low-lying placenta: Placenta is in lower segment but does not reach the os (C) Incomplete (partial): Placenta partially covers the os (D) Complete: Placenta completely covers the os

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with increased urine output. On evaluation, his urinary output was around 4 L/day; urinary osmolality was 200 mosmol/L. Which of the following are various differential diagnosis? I. Psychogenic polydipsia II. Solute diuresis III. Central diabetes insipidus IV. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, III and IV

Polyuria is defined as a urine output >3 L/day in adults. The first step in evaluating polyuria is to measure the urine osmolality.

This patient has:

• Urine output = 4 L/day (polyuria)
• Urine osmolality = 200 mOsm/kg (dilute urine)

A low urine osmolality (<300 mOsm/kg) indicates water diuresis, and the major differential diagnoses are:

• Psychogenic (primary) polydipsia
• Central diabetes insipidus (CDI)
• Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI)

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Solute diuresis

• Solute diuresis (e.g., uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, mannitol therapy, urea diuresis) produces high urine osmolality (>300 mOsm/kg) due to increased urinary solute excretion.
• Therefore, it is not consistent with a urine osmolality of 200 mOsm/kg.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Polyuria is defined as a urine output >3 L/day in adults. The first step in evaluating polyuria is to measure the urine osmolality.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following radiological image was taken to assess the urinary tract. Identify the investigation shown below.
questions.explanation: The image depicts an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), a contrast-enhanced study used to visualize the anatomy and functional state of the urinary tract. After IV contrast injection, it is filtered by the kidneys and excreted, allowing sequential imaging of the renal calyces, pelvis, ureters, and bladder. A pelvic X-ray (Option B) is a plain film that only shows bones and gross calcifications without visualizing soft tissue urinary structures. A retrograde pyelogram (Option C) involves contrast introduced via a catheter through the urethra, typically used when IV contrast is contraindicated. An MCUG (Option D) involves instilling contrast into the bladder to evaluate for vesicoureteral reflux during urination. Because the image shows the entire collecting system simultaneously via contrast excretion, it is a definitive IVP

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to casualty with seizures. He had multiple episodes and was taking herbal medicines for the same. He was conscious in between the episodes. During the episodes, he had arching of his back. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strychnine

The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of strychnine poisoning.

Strychnine poisoning occurs if a person ingests crushed seeds of Strychnos nux vomica. If swallowed uncrushed, the seeds of nux vomica have no poisonous action. The fatal dose is 15-30 mg of strychnine or one crushed seed.

Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine at the postganglionic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. This leads to increased activity in the motor neurons.

Patients typically present with

• Convulsions are clonic initially but eventually become tonic.
• Risus sardonicus results from the contraction of the jaws and facial muscles in which the corners of the mouth are drawn back.
• The convulsions are most marked in anti-gravity muscles so that the body typically arches in hyperextension, the posture known as opisthotonus.
• If the spasm involves the abdominal muscles, the body bends forward (emprosthotonos), or to the side (pleurosthotonus).
• If death is preceded by a severe convulsion, as in strychnine poisoning, it causes an increase in the body temperature known as postmortem caloricity.

The first step in the management of strychnine poisoning is to control convulsions with benzodiazepines or barbiturates to control seizures, and the patients should be placed in a dark room to avoid triggering further convulsions. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb unabsorbed poison after a thorough stomach wash. Acidification of urine can be done to increase the excretion of strychnine.

Other options:

Option B: Ricinus poisoning leads to symptoms such as the burning of the oral mucosa, salivation, nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. It may also cause drowsiness, convulsions, delirium, and death.

Option C: Nerium poisoning presents with headache, dizziness, respiratory difficulty, and nausea. Ingestion causes difficulty in swallowing and articulation, abdominal pain, vomiting, profuse frothy salivation, and diarrhea. Blood pressure falls, fibrillation, AV block, coma, respiratory paralysis, and death can occur due to cardiac failure.

Option D: Datura poisoning presents with

• Dry hot skin (Temperature rises up to 42°C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated)
• Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
• Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst
• Dysphagia
• Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels
• Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)
• Drunken gait
• Delirium
• Drowsiness
• Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure
questions.learning: Strychnine — The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of strychnine poisoning. Strychnine poisoning occurs if a person ingests crushed seeds of Strychnos nux vomica.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient whose diet predominantly consists of rice and pulses presents with bowed legs (stick deformity). Deficiency of which vitamin could have been prevented to avoid this condition?
questions.explanation: Bowed legs, also known as a "stick deformity," in a patient with a restricted diet are a classic sign of rickets, a disease caused by Vitamin D deficiency in children. Vitamin D is critical for the intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate; its absence leads to defective bone mineralization and soft, deformed bones. Pulses and rice are poor sources of Vitamin D compared to fortified dairy or fish liver oils. Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia, not bone deformities. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option B) causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological issues. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) leads to scurvy, which causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing but not the characteristic bowing of the legs. Sunlight exposure is the primary natural source of Vitamin D via endogenous skin synthesis
questions.learning: Bowed legs, also known as a "stick deformity," in a patient with a restricted diet are a classic sign of rickets, a disease caused by Vitamin D deficiency in children.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding folate deficiency is FALSE?
options: High homocysteine and normal methyl malonic acid
If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects
Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia
Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before supplementing folate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects

Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryonic development (between days 21–28 after conception, around the 4th week of gestation). By the time most women realize they are pregnant (usually 5–6 weeks gestation), neural tube closure has already occurred.

Therefore, folic acid must be taken before conception and continued through the first trimester to effectively reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs).

• Recommended dose for low-risk women: 400 µg/day, beginning at least 1 month before conception.
• High-risk women (previous pregnancy with NTD, certain antiepileptic drugs, etc.): 4–5 mg/day before conception.

Why are the other options correct

A. High homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid levels

Folate deficiency impairs the conversion of homocysteine → methionine, leading to:

• ↑ Homocysteine
• Normal methylmalonic acid (MMA)

In contrast:

| Deficiency | Homocysteine | Methylmalonic acid

| ---------- | ------------ | ------------------

| Folate deficiency | ↑ | Normal

| Vitamin B12 deficiency | ↑ | ↑

High-yield pearl: MMA differentiates vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

C. Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia

Children with chronic hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia) have:

• Increased RBC destruction
• Increased bone marrow activity
• Increased DNA synthesis
• Increased folate requirement

Hence, routine folate supplementation is recommended to support erythropoiesis.

D. Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before folate supplementation

This is an important clinical principle.

Giving folic acid alone to a patient with unrecognized vitamin B12 deficiency:

• Corrects the megaloblastic anemia
• Does not treat the neurological damage
• May allow neurological complications to progress unnoticed, sometimes irreversibly

Therefore:

• Always exclude or treat vitamin B12 deficiency first, or give both B12 and folate if both deficiencies are suspected.
questions.learning: If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryonic development (between days 21–28 after conception, around the 4th week of gestation).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man undergoing a routine health checkup is found to have hepatomegaly and an abnormally dark skin pigmentation despite minimal sun exposure. A liver biopsy has been performed, and the histological image is provided. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hepatomegaly and an unusually dark complexion (often described as "bronze diabetes" when combined with pancreatic damage) is the classic clinical presentation of hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis is an iron-overload disorder where excessive iron is deposited in various organs. The provided liver biopsy image shows hepatocytes filled with golden-brown granules, which are hemosiderin deposits. Wilson's disease (Option A) involves copper accumulation and would not cause a "tan". Autoimmune hepatitis (Option B) presents with lymphocytic infiltration rather than pigment deposits. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option C) is characterized by periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive diastase-resistant globules in the liver. Because the clinical triad of liver enlargement and skin hyperpigmentation, matched with microscopic iron deposits, is specific to iron overload, hemochromatosis is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of hepatomegaly and an unusually dark complexion (often described as "bronze diabetes" when combined with pancreatic damage) is the classic clinical presentation of hemochromatosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which conditions or factors are commonly linked to the development of rhino-cerebral mucormycosis, a serious fungal infection?
questions.explanation: Rhino-cerebral mucormycosis is a devastating, opportunistic fungal infection caused by members of the order Mucorales. The most common and potent clinical association for its development is Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). The fungus thrives in an environment of high glucose and acidic pH. Furthermore, the elevated levels of free iron in the blood during DKA act as a growth factor for the organism. Pregnancy (Option B) is not a primary risk factor. While broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option C) and systemic steroids can predispose individuals to various fungal infections, DKA is the classic, pathognomonic predisposing state for the specific necrotic, invasive "rhino-cerebral" presentation of mucormycosis. These fungi are angioinvasive, leading to rapid tissue infarction and death if glycemic control and surgical debridement are not initiated immediately. Therefore, DKA is the definitive metabolic state associated with this disease
questions.learning: Rhino-cerebral mucormycosis is a devastating, opportunistic fungal infection caused by members of the order Mucorales. The most common and potent clinical association for its development is Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A newborn baby presents with difficulty breathing. It is noted that his symptoms improve when he cries. In which disease does the symptom improve upon crying?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Choanal atresia

The given clinical scenario stridor in an infant that relieves on crying is suggestive of choanal atresia.

Improvement of stridor on crying is seen in gross obstruction like choanal atresia while laryngomalacia presents with worsening of stridor while crying or feeding. Sinusitis presents with stretor rather than stridor and it does not relieve while crying.

Choanal atresia is the persistence of the bucconasal membrane, unilateral is more common and may remain undiagnosed until adult life, bilateral atresia will present as a respiratory obstruction in the newborn. The initial clinical evaluation consists of placing a large laryngeal mirror under each nostril and checking for fogging, this is known as the laryngeal mirror test.

Diagnosis can be made by:

* Presence of mucoid discharge in the nose

* Absence of air bubbles in the nasal discharge

* Failure to pass a catheter from the nose to the pharynx

* Putting methylene blue dye into the nose and checking its passage to the pharynx

* Putting a radio-opaque dye into the nose and taking a lateral radiograph

* CT in the axial plane

Management: In bilateral atresia, emergency treatment is to provide an airway, which is done by McGovern's technique- (a feeding tube with a large hole that provides a good oral airway), this removes the need for tracheostomy. Definitive treatment is correcting the atresia either by trans palatal or transnasal approach, which is usually done at one and a half years of age.

Pearl PF1080: Choanal atresia

* It is due to the persistence of bucconasal membrane which separates primitive oropharynx from the primitive nasopharynx

* Unilateral > bilateral

* 30% of cases are bony and 70% are mixed

* Unilateral cases may be asymptomatic and present in adult life

* Bilateral cases are life-threatening and present with respiratory distress

* Associated with CHARGE syndrome

* C- Coloboma of the eye

* H- Heart defects

* A- Atresia of choana

* R- Retarded growth and development

* G- Genital anomalies

* E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

* CT scan is the best investigation

Image: Membranous, bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn

* McGoverns technique- A feeding nipple with a large hole provides a good oral airway

* Definitive treatment consists of correction of atresia by a trans-nasal or trans-palatal approach.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Zika virus is transmitted by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aedes aegypti

Zika virus may be transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus.

The symptoms of Zika virus disease include fever, rash, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, or headache. These symptoms are mild and usually last for 2-7 days.

It can spread via:

* Mosquito bites

* Bloodstream

* Unsafe sexual practices

* Vertical transmission

Zika virus infection during pregnancy may lead to microcephaly or congenital Zika syndrome.

The complications include:

* Guillain-Barré syndrome

* Encephalitis

* Meningitis

* Myelitis

* Mosquitoes are global in distribution.

* The main species of mosquitoes include the Anopheles, Culex, Aedes and Mansonia.

* Flight range varies up to 11 kms, except Aedes for which it is 100 metres.

* Life span of mosquitoes is around 8 to 34 days.

* Their morphology consists of a head with a proboscis, a pair of palpi and a pair of antennae; a thorax and an abdomen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is part of the WHO criteria for Severe Acute Malnutrition(SAM)?
options: Mid-upper arm circumference less than 11 cm
Mid-upper arm circumference less than 12 cm
Mid-upper arm circumference less than 12.5 cm
Mid-upper arm circumference less than 11.5 cm
questions.explanation:

* Presence of bipedal edema

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with Hb 6.3 with a history of repeated blood transfusions. Investigations show MCV- 70 fl and the peripheral smear showed a hypochromic microcytic picture. Which of the following investigations should be done next in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hb electrophoresis

The given clinical scenario of repeated transfusions, low Hb, low MCV, and a hypochromic microcytic picture in the smear is suggestive of thalassemia and Hb electrophoresis should be done in this for diagnosis.

Hb Electrophoresis is used for newborn screening. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is the investigation of choice but is not as definitive as globin gene sequencing.

Each individual carries 2 beta-chain genes and 4 alpha-chain genes.

Haemoglobin levels:

* Normal hemoglobin pattern- HbA=95%, HbA2=3.5%, HbF =1.5%

* Beta-thalassemia trait- HbA=90%, HbA2=5%, HbF=5%

* Beta-thalassemia intermedia- HbA=45%, HbA2=5%, HbF=50%

Clinical features in thalassemia:

* Anaemia

* Jaundice and pigment gallstones

* Skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, osteopenia/osteoporosis

* Iron overload

* Growth impairment

* Hepatosplenomegaly

* Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus

* Heart failure and arrhythmias

Laboratory studies:

* Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anaemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases. These findings are non-specific.

* High RBC count

* Low reticulocyte count

* ↑ LDH

* High transferrin saturation, normal serum iron levels, elevated ferritin levels

Other options:

Option A: Measurement of serum iron is necessary to monitor for iron overload in case of repeated blood transfusion. But in this case, the first step is to confirm the diagnosis by doing Hb electrophoresis.

Option B: Direct Coomb's test is used to test for AIHA- Autoimmune hemolytic anaemia. Given the history, AIHA seems unlikely and it usually occurs in adults and is unusual in a child.

Option C: Osmotic fragility test is a test done in the case of hereditary spherocytosis. It presents with splenomegaly, anemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. The MCV is decreased and MCHC is increased due to dehydration. It is unlikely to have a history of chronic blood transfusion.

Pearl PF0864: Thalassemia syndromes

Normally each individual carries 4 functional alpha chain genes and 2 functional beta chain genes. Alpha and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively.

* Alpha thalassemia: Gene deletion is the most common cause of reduced α-chain synthesis.

* Beta +- thalassemia: The most common cause is splicing mutation.

* Beta 0- thalassemia: Chain terminator mutations are the most common cause.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Greater auricular nerve

The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the preauricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario.

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in patients with severe vomiting?
questions.explanation: Severe vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), resulting in metabolic alkalosis. This alkalosis causes an intracellular shift of potassium, which, combined with increased renal potassium excretion to compensate for the bicarbonate load, leads to profound hypokalemia. Low serum potassium disrupts the cardiac membrane potential and repolarization, making it a major risk factor for life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Typical ECG changes in hypokalemia include flattened T waves, prominent U waves, and a prolonged QT interval, which can lead to Torsades de Pointes. Hyponatremia (Option B) can occur due to volume loss but is less likely to cause direct arrhythmias. Hyperkalemia (Option C) typically results from renal failure or acidosis, not vomiting. Hypocalcemia (Option D) causes QT prolongation and tetany but is not the primary drive for arrhythmias in the setting of gastric acid loss. Treatment focuses on replacing potassium and correcting the underlying fluid deficit

Anatomical dead space can be measured by the single-breath N2 curve (Fowler's method).

• Anatomical dead space is the respiratory system volume exclusive of alveoli.
• Alveolar dead space is the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood i.e. wasted ventilation.
• Physiological/total dead space is the sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space.
• The equation used for the calculation of total/physiological dead space is the Bohr’s equation.

From I–II is a mixture of DS and alveolar gas.

questions.text: Which is the study design of choice for finding out circadian variation of fat content in expressed breast milk of mother of preterm babies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prospective Cohort

The study of choice is a prospective study.

In the above scenario, the study group would consist of the mothers of preterm babies, while the comparison group would consist of the mothers of term babies. To study the circadian variation of the fat content in the expressed breast milk, the samples of breast milk would be taken at specific time intervals every day and followed up for several days and would be analyzed. This is a prospective study.

Other options:

Option b: An ambispective cohort is the combination of both retrospective and prospective cohort studies.

Option c: In a case-control study, the study begins from the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.

Option d: Cross-sectional study is done to identify the prevalence of a disease.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following treatment modalities is most commonly employed for managing recurrent pterygium of the eye?
questions.explanation: A pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular growth of the conjunctiva onto the cornea. The primary challenge in pterygium surgery is the high rate of recurrence. For recurrent pterygium, "Conjunctival Autografting" (CAG) is the gold standard and most frequently used technique. This involves harvesting healthy conjunctiva from another part of the eye and suturing or gluing it over the site where the pterygium was removed. Option D (Bare sclera technique) has an unacceptably high recurrence rate and is rarely used alone. Option B (Beta-radiation) and Option C (Observation) are either outdated due to complications or ineffective for an active, recurrent growth. CAG significantly reduces the recurrence rate to less than 5–10%. Mitomycin-C is also sometimes used as an adjunct, but autografting remains the preferred surgical choice for providing a long-term, stable ocular surface and superior cosmetic results
questions.learning: A pterygium is a triangular fibrovascular growth of the conjunctiva onto the cornea. The primary challenge in pterygium surgery is the high rate of recurrence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 16-year-old female presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain and a history of passing blood in stools. On examination, she has dark pigmented spots on her lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

The clinical scenario of passage of blood in stools with mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark pigmented spots on lips and oral mucosa) and the presence of hamartomatous polyps in the small intestines in endoscopy is highly suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. Due to germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the gene STK11. The hyperpigmentation typically appears as dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of the hands, genitalia, and perianal region.

Complications:

* Intussusception

* Risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers.

Treatment of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome mainly involves resection of polyps when there is heavy, persistent, or recurrent bleeding, or if intussusception develops. Polyps may be removed surgically by enterotomy or laparotomy, or endoscopically using a colonoscope introduced via an enterotomy. In severe cases where large segments of the small intestine are involved, resection of the affected portion may be required.

Other options:

Option A: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder presenting with numerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of FAP.

Option C: Juvenile polyposis (JPS) is an autosomal dominant inherited condition that presents with hamartomatous polyps due to mutations in the BMPR1A, SMAD4 or ENG genes. Pigmentation is not present.

Option D: Cowden disease is characterised by polyps of stomach or colon with mucocutaneous lesions, thyroid adenomas and goitre, fibroadenomas and fibrocystic disease of the breast, Uterine leiomyomas, macrocephaly.

Pearl PF0932: Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

* Autosomal-dominant disease

* Germline defects in the tumor suppressor serine-threonine kinase 11 (STK11) gene on chromosome 19.

Features:

* Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, and digits

* Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract

* Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum.

* Increased risk for extraintestinal malignant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles.

Screening: Baseline colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age 20 years, followed by annual flexible sigmoidoscopy thereafter.

Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gastrointestinal manifestations:

* Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100

* Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases.

* Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma.

* Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant

Extraintestinal manifestations

* Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

* Epidermoid cysts

* Desmoid tumors in the abdomen

* Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia

* Brain tumors

* Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient undergoing cardiac surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cefazolin

First- and second-generation cephalosporins (cefazolin) are the drugs of choice for preoperative prophylaxis for cardiac surgery. Clindamycin is reserved for cases of allergy to beta-lactams and vancomycin is recommended for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is essential in reducing the risk of surgical site infections, particularly in cardiac surgery, where the consequences of infection can be severe. The choice of antibiotic depends on the patient's medical history, allergies, and the most common pathogens involved in surgical site infections for the specific surgery. In addition to cefazolin, other cephalosporins, such as cefuroxime, can also be used for prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. The timing of antibiotic administration is crucial, with the first dose typically given within 60 minutes before the incision.

Other Options:

Option A: Penicillin G is not the drug of choice for preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is mainly used to treat infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria, such as Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and some strains of Staphylococcus aureus.

Option B: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic and is not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is typically used to treat respiratory tract infections, skin infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria.

Option C: Azithromycin, another macrolide antibiotic, is also not the drug of choice for preoperative prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. It is commonly used to treat respiratory tract infections, sexually transmitted infections, and other infections caused by susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

questions.text: A patient with hemophilia on antiretroviral therapy is brought in altered mental status following complaints of nausea, vomiting and headache. Which of the following medications was he taking?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tipranavir

This patient was most likely taking tipranavir, as it is known to be associated with an increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage and hepatotoxicity which is the likely cause of altered mental status in this patient with hemophilia following complaints of nausea, vomiting and headache.
Tipranavir is a protease inhibitor (PI) used in patients who are resistant to other PIs. It is often combined with ritonavir, to achieve better therapeutic outcomes. It should be avoided in patients with head trauma or bleeding diathesis, such as hemophilia as it is associated with an increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage. Other common adverse effects of tipranavir include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, urticarial or maculopapular rash, and liver toxicity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which of the following causes increased glutamine in blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ornithine transcarbamoylase

Deficiency ornithine transcarbamoylase causes increased glutamine in blood

Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline in the urea cycle. Its deficiency leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate. The carbamoyl phosphate is then shunted to pyrimidine biosynthesis, resulting in high ammonia and orotic acid levels in the blood. This condition is thus called hyperammonemia type 2.

As a compensatory mechanism, ammonia is then combined with glutamate to form glutamine (by the enzyme glutamine synthetase). The levels of glutamine are elevated in the blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and urine, probably as a result of this dysregulated glutamine synthesis.

Other options:

Option A: Deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase leads to argininosuccinic aciduria

Option C: Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase-A leads to Fabry’s disease and an accumulation of globotriaosylceramide.

Option D: Deficiency of arginase leads to hyperargininemia

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—mouth breathing, an elongated expressionless face ("adenoid facies"), a high-arched palate, and crowded teeth—is pathognomonic for chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy . The adenoids are lymphoid tissues in the nasopharynx; when enlarged, they block the posterior choanae, forcing the child to breathe through the mouth. This chronic mouth breathing leads to the characteristic craniofacial changes described. Lingual tonsils (Option A) are at the base of the tongue and do not cause nasal obstruction. Quinsy (Option B) is a peritonsillar abscess causing acute throat pain. Tonsillar hypertrophy (Option C) involves enlarged palatine tonsils, which can cause snoring and dysphagia but are less typically associated with the "adenoid facies" skeletal changes . The provided X-ray likely shows a soft tissue mass in the nasopharynx narrowing the airway. Consequently, adenoid hypertrophy is the most accurate diagnosis for this 5-year-old child

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Bubo is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: A bubo is a painful, markedly swollen lymph node, typically in the groin or axilla. It is a characteristic feature of Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), a sexually transmitted infection caused by specific serotypes (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis. In LGV, the buboes are often divided by the inguinal ligament, creating the pathognomonic "Groove sign." Herpes simplex (Option B) causes multiple painful superficial ulcers and mild lymphadenopathy, not massive buboes. Primary syphilis (Option C) presents with a painless chancre and painless, rubbery lymph nodes. Donovanosis (Option D) presents with painless, "beefy-red" ulcers and pseudo-buboes (granulomatous swelling in the groin), rather than true lymph node involvement. Buboes are also the hallmark of the bubonic plague. Identifying the nature of the inguinal swelling is essential for differentiating STIs and initiating correct antimicrobial therapy, such as doxycycline for LGV

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with head and neck cancer was told by his oncologist that needs radiotherapy at a total dose of 70 Gy over a 7 week period for his tumor. He was scheduled to receive a dose of 1.8-2Gy per fraction, once daily over 5 days a week, for 7 weeks. What is this type of radiotherapy called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumour is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximises the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimises the damage on the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumour cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells who were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumour cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

* In the case of Head and neck cancer, the conventional schedule of radiotherapy involves the delivery of 70 Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions(total around 35-36 fractions) over 7 weeks, treating 5 days per week.

* However, this dose can be delivered at 1.10-1.25 Gy/fraction for 56 fractions over the same time period of 7 weeks which is called hyperfractionation(Option B). This delivers a lower dose with more fractions and the efficacy improves as the healthy cells have more ability to repair themselves in the intervening time.

* Accelerated fractionation(Option C) is when the same 70 Gy, is given at around 1.6-1.8 Gy/fraction but it is delivered more than once daily, decreasing the total treatment time to around 6 weeks. These aim to decrease tumor proliferation which can lead to failure of the therapy.

Note:

* Shorter schedules remain useful for small-volume treatments: 50 Gy in 16 fractions over 3 weeks or 55 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks.

* Accelerated schedules although is easier to implement than hyperfractionation result in a lesser survival gain.

Option D: Brachytherapy is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.

The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy:

* I-125 and Iridium-192 - are used in low-dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy.

* Cobalt-60 - is used for high-dose rate (HDR) brachytherapy.

Afterloading is the process of placing the radioactive material into the target region. This is either done manually by the oncologist, or by using remote afterloading devices.

Remote afterloading devices enable us to eliminate direct contact with radioactive sources while administration. It provides protection from radiation exposure to healthcare professionals by securing the radiation source in a shielded safe manner.
questions.learning: Regular Fractionated radiotherapy Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a seat belt injury, which of the following organs is most commonly affected?
questions.explanation: The "seat belt sign"—a pattern of bruising on the abdomen or chest—is a critical indicator of potential internal damage following a high-velocity collision. In patients with this sign, the most commonly affected internal organs are the hollow viscera, particularly the small intestine and the mesentery. The sudden deceleration forces the belt to compress the abdominal contents, leading to shearing or burst injuries of the bowel. While the spleen (Option B) and liver (Option A) are the most commonly injured organs in general blunt abdominal trauma, the specific mechanism of seat belt compression significantly increases the risk of a hollow viscus injury compared to solid organs. Pancreatic injuries (Option C) are rarer and usually result from direct compression against the vertebral column. Clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for delayed bowel perforation in these patients, as early CT scans may be inconclusive. Observation and repeated physical examinations are essential to detect signs of peritonitis that necessitate urgent surgical exploration
questions.learning: The "seat belt sign"—a pattern of bruising on the abdomen or chest—is a critical indicator of potential internal damage following a high-velocity collision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Xeropthalmia is considered a public health problem if the prevalence of bitot spot is more than?
questions.explanation: According to WHO and national guidelines, xerophthalmia (the ocular manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency) is classified as a significant public health problem in a community based on specific prevalence thresholds. For Bitot's spots (X1B stage), the threshold is a prevalence of more than 0.5% among the preschool-age child population. Other thresholds include night blindness (XN) > 1%, conjunctival xerosis (X1A) > 0.01%, and corneal xerosis/ulceration (X2/X3) > 0.01%. Options A (0.01%), B (0.05%), and D (1%) are incorrect values for the Bitot spot criteria. Reaching or exceeding these thresholds signals the need for urgent community-wide interventions, such as universal Vitamin A supplementation, fortification of food staples, and intensive health education. These prevalence surveys are vital for monitoring the effectiveness of nutrition programs and identifying high-risk geographic areas. Eradicating xerophthalmia is a primary goal in pediatric public health to prevent avoidable childhood blindness and reduce overall childhood mortality
questions.learning: According to WHO and national guidelines, xerophthalmia (the ocular manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency) is classified as a significant public health problem in a community based on specific prevalence thresholds.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever for the past 2 months. General examination showed pallor and the systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level- 3 gm/dl, TLC- 1500/microL, platelet count- 15000/microL. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte count is 0.5. Bone marrow examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but no immature cells. What is the likely diagnosis? Hb- Hemoglobin TLC- Total leucocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia

The given clinical scenario showing a young male with gum bleeding, fever, pancytopenia, and a low reticulocyte count with bone marrow showing fatty streaks and no immature cells is suggestive of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia.

Aplastic anemia is a syndrome characterized by chronic hematopoietic failure and pancytopenia. The common causes include:

* Acquired

* Idiopathic (most common cause, about 65% of the cases)

* Acquired stem-cell defects

* Immune-mediated

* Chemical agents

* Dose-related (alkylating agents, antimetabolites, benzene, chloramphenicol, inorganic arsenals)

* Idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, organic arsenicals, carbamazepine, penicillamine, gold salts)

* Physical agents

* Whole-body irradiation

* Viral infections (hepatitis, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Varicella-Zoster virus)

* Inherited

* Fanconi anemia

* Telomerase defects

Pathogenesis involves an extrinsic immune-mediated suppression of bone marrow and an intrinsic abnormality of the stem cells.

Clinical features and diagnosis:

There is no age or sex predisposition for aplastic anemia. It presents insidiously with features of pancytopenia such as pallor, petechiae, and ecchymosis. Recurrent infections and fever occur as a result of neutropenia. Reticulocytopenia is seen and splenomegaly is characteristically absent. Bone marrow biopsy is used for diagnosis.

Histology:

Bone marrow aspirate usually results in a dry tap. Examination shows a hypocellular marrow devoid of hematopoietic cells with remnant fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes. Red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. The following image shows a hypocellular bone marrow with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells.

Other options:

Option B - Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. Red cells deficient in these proteins are susceptible to intravascular hemolysis. Patients with PNH usually present with pancytopenia and reticulocytosis with bone marrow biopsy showing a cellular marrow with marked to massive erythroid hyperplasia.

Option C - Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal stem cell disorders. It is a consequence of maturation defects that result in ineffective hematopoiesis with a high predisposition to conversion to AML. They are characterized by a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic cells on bone marrow aspirate. Marrow changes seen in MDS are given in the pearl below.

Option D - Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

Pearl PF0598: Marrow Changes in Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)

The myelodysplastic syndrome can lead to dysplasia of the erythroid series, myeloid series, and megakaryocytes.

Dysplasia of erythroid series appears as

* Ring sideroblasts- Erythroblasts with stainable iron in the cytoplasm

* Megaloblastoid maturation- Abnormally large erythroid cells

* Nuclear budding abnormalities- Nucleus with abnormal shape

Dysplasia of myeloid series

* Neutrophils with a decreased number of secondary granules

* Pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells- neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes

Dysplasia of the megakaryocytes-

* Megakaryocyte with single nuclear lobe

* Pawn ball megakaryocytes- cells with multiple separate nuclei

If only one lineage is affected, then it is called single lineage dysplasia. If multiple lineages are affected, then it is called multilineage dysplasia. If the percentage of ring sideroblasts is more than 15% it is called MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ventouse is contraindicated in which of the following subsequent circumstances?
questions.explanation: A Ventouse (vacuum extractor) is an instrument used to assist in vaginal delivery. It is indicated for a prolonged second stage of labor (Option A), maternal exhaustion (Option B), or acute fetal distress (Option C) when the head is deeply engaged. However, its use is strictly contraindicated in a premature baby (Option D), typically defined as less than 34 weeks of gestation. The premature fetal skull is softer and the scalp more fragile, making the infant highly susceptible to intracranial hemorrhage, subgaleal hematoma, and scalp lacerations from the suction cup. Other contraindications include malpresentations like face or breech, or when fetal blood sampling has recently been performed (increasing bleeding risk). In the case of prematurity, if instrumental assistance is required, forceps are generally preferred as they protect the fetal head rather than applying suction to it. Therefore, prematurity is a critical contraindication for vacuum-assisted delivery
questions.learning: A Ventouse (vacuum extractor) is an instrument used to assist in vaginal delivery. It is indicated for a prolonged second stage of labor (Option A), maternal exhaustion (Option B), or acute fetal distress (Option C) when the head is deeply engaged.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about Palonosetron are incorrect?
options: It is a second generation 5HT3 receptor antagonist
It belongs to the class of most effective drugs for chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting
It is the longest acting drug amongst its class
High risk of QT prolongation as adverse reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High risk of QT prolongation as adverse reaction

Palonosetron is a second-generation 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist used primarily for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV).

• Higher receptor affinity and long half-life (\~40 hours) compared to first-generation agents (ondansetron, granisetron).
• Most effective for delayed CINV.
• Longest acting drug in the 5-HT₃ antagonist class.

Safety profile:

• Unlike earlier 5-HT₃ antagonists, palonosetron has minimal risk of QT interval prolongation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a pupil that remains constricted even in dim light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis (lack of sweating), and mild ptosis (due to Müller muscle weakness) defines Horner syndrome. This condition results from a disruption in the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye. The pupil remains small even in low light because the sympathetic dilator fibers are non-functional. Adie's tonic pupil (Option A) typically presents with a dilated (mydriatic) pupil that is sluggishly reactive to light. Marcus Gunn pupil (Option C), or a relative afferent pupillary defect, is characterized by paradoxical dilation when light is swung from the normal to the affected eye. Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D), associated with tertiary syphilis, features bilateral small pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. Because the patient’s symptoms specifically include ipsilateral ptosis and anhidrosis alongside the small pupil, Horner syndrome is the most accurate clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The classic triad of miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis (lack of sweating), and mild ptosis (due to Müller muscle weakness) defines Horner syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman brings her daughter alleging a history of sexual assault. The mother claims the girl is under 18, but the doctor suspects otherwise. Which X-ray investigation can assist in determining if the girl is over 18 years based on epiphyseal fusion?
options: Medial end of clavicle, wrist and pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial end of clavicle, wrist and pelvis

Age determination around 18 years relies on assessing late-fusing epiphyses.

The medial end of clavicle is the most reliable indicator at this threshold (secondary center appears \~18 years, fuses \~21 years).

Wrist (radius/ulna) and pelvic epiphyses (iliac crest, ischial tuberosity, femoral head) provide supportive evidence, as their fusion spans 17–21 years.

Elbow/shoulder fuse earlier, sternum has a wide fusion range, and skull sutures are irrelevant—hence medial end of clavicle + wrist + pelvis is optimal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with a history of complex endometrial hyperplasia, an endometrial thickness of 14 mm, an adnexal mass, and atypical cells on evaluation?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypical cells and an endometrial thickness of 14mm significantly increases the risk of underlying endometrial carcinoma. The presence of a concurrent adnexal mass in this clinical context strongly suggests the spread of the malignancy to the ovary. Metastasis from endometrial cancer is a well-recognized cause of secondary ovarian tumors. Struma ovarii (Option A) is a rare specialized germ cell tumor containing thyroid tissue, which does not correlate with endometrial hyperplasia. Polycystic ovarian disease (Option C) presents with chronic anovulation and polycystic morphology on USG, not typically an adnexal mass alongside complex atypical hyperplasia. Immature ovarian teratoma (Option D) is a germ cell malignancy seen in younger patients and lacks the direct association with thickened endometrium. Thus, given the uterine pathology, metastatic endometrial cancer to the ovary is the most probable clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient's history of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypical cells and an endometrial thickness of 14mm significantly increases the risk of underlying endometrial carcinoma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the provided population pyramid indicate, with the exception of?
questions.explanation: The population pyramid shown features a broad base that rapidly tapers toward a narrow apex. This "expansive" shape indicates high birth rates and high death rates. Such pyramids are characteristic of developing countries (Option A) where there is a "more young population" (Option C) and the total population is rapidly increasing (Option D). In contrast, developed countries (Option B) typically have a "constrictive" or "stationary" pyramid with a narrower base (low birth rates) and a more vertical shape, representing an aging population and low growth. Because the visual data clearly represents a young, growing, high-fertility demographic typical of less developed regions, the "developed countries" label is the incorrect description and thus the correct "except" choice for this question
questions.learning: The population pyramid shown features a broad base that rapidly tapers toward a narrow apex. This "expansive" shape indicates high birth rates and high death rates.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the reason that hemoglobin cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state?
options: It is a large molecule bounded with another protein.
It gets attracted to the positive charge of the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a large molecule bounded with another protein.

The haemoglobin (Hb) cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state because it is a large molecule bound with another protein.

The Hb molecule released into the blood from RBCs is immediately bound by a protein called haptoglobin (size: 12.4 nm). It forms the haemoglobin-haptoglobin complex which is large enough to be prevented from crossing the glomerular filtration barrier.

Free haemoglobin undergoes extensive glomerular filtration, which is blocked by Haptoglobin. The filtration of Hb leads to renal tubule iron deposition (brown) and hemoglobinuria. This is prevented by the sequestration of Hb by haptoglobin.

Another reason is because of the negative charge of Hb. Both the Hb and glomerular filtration barrier are negatively charged. Hence Hb is repelled away from the filtration barrier.

The glomerular filtration barrier consists of:

* The endothelium of the capillary

* A basement membrane - contains type IV collagen, glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge.

* A layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane.

The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, which measure from 4 nm up to 8nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of less than 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approaches zero.

In addition to the size of the particles, the filtration also depends mainly on the charge of the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively charged proteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most of the negative charges (anionic substances). Whereas, the cationic substances are easily filtered.
questions.learning: It is a large molecule bounded with another protein. The haemoglobin (Hb) cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state because it is a large molecule bound with another protein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding vasectomy?
options: The procedure is done under local anesthesia.
Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure.
A no-scalpel technique is being widely used now.
The vas deferens is the structure that is divided in the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure.

Option B is incorrect as sperms can remain in the reproductive tract for up to 3 months and thus sterility is not immediate. It can take up to 3 months after the procedure and during this time period, the couple must abstain from intercourse or use other methods of contraception.

Vasectomy:

Vasectomy is done under local anaesthesia. A small incision is made in the scrotum. The vas deferens are divided on both sides which disrupts the passage of sperms.

The no-scalpel technique has been now adopted. One single incision is made with special forceps and skin stitch is not required. Clips and plugs can be applied over the vas instead of cutting.

Approximately, 20 ejaculates clear the semen of all sperms. Two semen analysis reports must confirm the absence of sperms before the man can be declared sterile.
questions.learning: Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure. Option B is incorrect as sperms can remain in the reproductive tract for up to 3 months and thus sterility is not immediate.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 23-year-old male presents with a lifelong history of easy bruising and mucosal bleeding. He reports frequent nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. Platelet count is normal. What is the most likely underlying defect responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gp Ib/IX complex deficiency

This patient has Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a congenital platelet adhesion disorder caused by deficiency of the Gp Ib/IX complex.

Clinical features:

• Mucocutaneous bleeding
• Epistaxis
• Easy bruising
• Prolonged bleeding after minor trauma

Laboratory findings:

• Normal platelet count or mild thrombocytopenia
• Giant platelets on peripheral smear
• Increased bleeding time
• Failure of ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation that does not correct with normal plasma

Important differentials:

• Glanzmann thrombasthenia → Gp IIb/IIIa defect → impaired platelet aggregation
• von Willebrand disease → vWF deficiency
• Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) → deep tissue/joint bleeding, not mucosal bleeding
questions.learning: Gp Ib/IX complex deficiency — This patient has Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a congenital platelet adhesion disorder caused by deficiency of the Gp Ib/IX complex.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the class of immunoglobulin shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ig A

The above image shows a dimeric structure, characteristic of secretory IgA.

IgA immunoglobulin is the major antibody responsible for mucosal immunity. Its serum levels are usually low. It is predominantly present in the extravascular secretions. It is present in secretions such as milk, saliva, and tears, and in secretions of the respiratory, intestinal, and genital tracts.

When present in the serum, it exists as a monomer similar to IgG. However, when it is secreted, it exists as a dimer. The dimeric structure consists of two monomers, which are stabilized by two additional polypeptides:

• J chain, which stabilizes the molecule.
• Secretory component, which is incorporated into the IgA when transported through the epithelial cell.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The eye examination of a 20-year-old male shows a golden ring on the iris. What is the next investigation to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum ceruloplasmin

The given image shows a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is seen in Wilson's disease. Low serum ceruloplasmin level is diagnostic of Wilson's disease.

Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an inherited metabolic disorder resulting due to abnormal copper deposition in tissues (mainly the liver and brain). It is caused by a deficiency of ceruloplasmin (copper-carrying blood protein).

Kayer-Fleischer ring is a brownish-yellow zone of copper deposition that is present in the peripheral Descemet membrane.

The ring is best seen on gonioscopy. Penicillamine therapy may cause the ring to disappear.

Another ocular finding in Wilson's disease is anterior capsular sunflower cataract.

Other options:

Option A: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leads to lung and liver disease.

Option B: Alpha-fetoprotein is a diagnostic marker in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Option C: Serum iron level is assessed in hemochromatosis which occurs due to increased iron deposition in various tissues. The ocular manifestation includes dry eye and rusty-brown perilimbal and conjunctival discoloration.
questions.learning: Serum ceruloplasmin — The given image shows a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is seen in Wilson's disease. Low serum ceruloplasmin level is diagnostic of Wilson's disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with episodic head-shaking movements since infancy, progressive gait instability, and mild cognitive impairment. There is no history of vomiting or macrocephaly. Neurological examination reveals truncal ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination. MRI brain (coronal T2-weighted image shown) demonstrated below. Which of the following neuroanatomical abnormalities best explains the embryological basis of this condition?
options: Failure of dorsal induction leading to holoprosencephaly
Failure of segmentation of the rhombic lips causing midline fusion of cerebellar hemispheres
Abnormal neural crest migration affecting posterior fossa development
Defective canalization of the fourth ventricle leading to cyst formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Failure of segmentation of the rhombic lips causing midline fusion of cerebellar hemispheres

Rhombencephalosynapsis is a rare hindbrain malformation characterized by agenesis of the cerebellar vermis with fusion of the cerebellar hemispheres, resulting from failure of midline cleavage of the rhombic lips during embryogenesis.

• MRI hallmark: single-lobed cerebellum with absent vermis and fused hemispheres
• Associated structural feature: fusion of dentate nuclei and superior cerebellar peduncles
• Fourth ventricle: typically narrow, slit-like, or keyhole-shaped
• Clinical clue: persistent head-shaking stereotypies + truncal ataxia (very characteristic)

Differentiation:

• vs Dandy–Walker → enlarged posterior fossa + cystic dilation of 4th ventricle
• vs Joubert syndrome → molar tooth sign (not fusion)

This condition represents a failure of cerebellar midline patterning, not a cystic or obstructive posterior fossa anomaly.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An abdominal mass in a patient with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is best seen _________.
options: During palpation over the left hypochondrium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. During feeding

In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, when the infant is given a test feed, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

All infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are evaluated with an ultrasound (investigation of choice). It confirms the diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Management: Rehydration and metabolic correction prior to definitive surgery - Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy.
questions.learning: During feeding — In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding ABO blood grouping?
options: Antibodies are naturally present since birth
The antigens are carbohydrate in nature
Antibodies are present only if antigens are absent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antibodies are naturally present since birth

Antibodies are not present since birth. At 2 to 8 months after birth, an infant begins to produce agglutinins (antibodies).

In the absence of type A agglutinogen(antigen) in an individual's RBCs, antibodies called anti-A agglutinins form in the plasma. Similarly, when type B agglutinogen is lacking in the RBCs, antibodies referred to as anti-B agglutinins develop in the plasma. Type A blood carries type A agglutinogens and anti-B agglutinins, while type B blood contains type B agglutinogens and anti-A agglutinins. Type AB blood possesses both A and B agglutinogens but no agglutinins. On the other hand, type O blood, which lacks agglutinogens, does have both anti-A and anti-B agglutinins.

The A and B antigens are complex oligosaccharides that differ in their terminal sugar. The agglutinins are gamma globulins produced by the bone marrow and lymph gland cells. Most of them are IgM and IgG immunoglobulin molecules.
questions.learning: Antibodies are naturally present since birth Antibodies are not present since birth. At 2 to 8 months after birth, an infant begins to produce agglutinins (antibodies).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A long-term study observed that individuals with high blood pressure in childhood tended to have high blood pressure in adulthood, while those with low childhood blood pressure generally maintained lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Tracking of blood pressure refers to the epidemiological phenomenon where an individual's relative position or "rank" within a population distribution remains consistent over time. For example, a child whose BP is at the 90th percentile for their age is statistically likely to remain at the high end of the BP distribution as an adult. This concept is vital for identifying future cardiovascular risk and implementing early prevention. The Rule of Halves (Option A) relates to the under-diagnosis and under-treatment of hypertension in a community. Regression to the mean (Option B) is a statistical concept where extreme measurements tend to move closer to the average upon repeat testing. A cohort effect (Option D) refers to shared characteristics or outcomes in a group based on their time of birth or shared experiences. Only "tracking" accurately describes the lifelong persistence of BP status
questions.learning: Tracking of blood pressure refers to the epidemiological phenomenon where an individual's relative position or "rank" within a population distribution remains consistent over time.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with progressively worsening dysphagia for both solids and liquids. Esophageal manometry shows absent or uncoordinated peristalsis and elevated resting pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and physiological profile provided is diagnostic for Achalasia Cardia. Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the hallmark manometric triad: aperistalsis (absent contractions), failure of the LES to relax, and elevated resting LES pressure. Clinically, it presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset, which distinguishes it from esophageal cancer (Option B), where dysphagia typically starts with solids and progresses to liquids. Stomach cancer (Option A) and GERD (Option C) do not produce these specific manometric findings. Barium swallow in achalasia characteristically shows a "bird's beak" appearance due to the persistent narrowing at the GE junction. Management options include pneumatic balloon dilation, botulinum toxin injections, or definitive surgical Heller's myotomy (often performed laparoscopically with a partial fundoplication). While more common in younger adults, achalasia can certainly occur in the elderly and must be differentiated from "pseudoachalasia" caused by a tumor at the cardia
