questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with complaints of pain and limping. The symptoms started 6 months back and gradually worsened. The child appears to be healthy with normal height and weight. On examination, there is mild wasting on the right side. Abduction (especially in flexion) and internal rotation are limited due to pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perthes disease

A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease. The image shows a mushroom-shaped femoral head that is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

Between 4 and 7 years of age, the femoral head may depend on the lateral epiphyseal vessels for its blood supply and venous drainage almost entirely. These vessels situated in the retinacula make them susceptible to stretching and to pressure from an effusion.

The disease is characterized by the disruption of blood flow to the head of the femur. Due to which the bone goes for osteonecrosis and stops growing. Over time, healing occurs by new blood vessels infiltrating the dead bone and removing the necrotic bone which leads to a loss of bone mass and a weakening of the femoral head. Clinical features include a boy of 4-8 years complaining of pain and limping. Symptoms continue for weeks on end or recur intermittently. The hip looks deceptively normal. Although initially, all movements are painful; with time, abduction with internal rotation is always limited.

Xray findings depend on the stages

* Necrotic phase: Radiographically dense areas which indicate new bone formation is soon followed by bone necrosis.

* Fragmentation phase: Alternating patches of density and lucency. Sometimes a crescentic subarticular fracture is often seen in lateral view

* Re-ossification phase: Epiphyseal density increases in this phase

* Healing phase: Normal femoral head or mushroom-shaped femoral head which is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

There are different 'head at risk signs' described by Catrell which include:

* lateral subluxation of the femoral head

* speckled calcification in the lateral epiphysis

* Epiphysis being horizontal

* Gage's sign: V-shaped osteoporotic segment in the lateral epiphysis and adjacent metaphysis.

Guidelines to treatment are derived from the review by Herring,

* Children under 6 years - symptomatic treatment including activity modification is appropriate

* Children aged 6-8 years - Bonge age and Catterall Staging determines the modality of treatment. Options include abduction brace or osteotomy.

* For children aged 9 and above - operative containment is the choice.

Note:Salter's extrusion angle helps to assess the femoral head extrusion. Normal is 50 degrees or more.
questions.learning: Perthes disease — A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which modification will lead to a change in the biological activity of the hormone given in the picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Change in 29-30 in B chain

The hormone shown in the above image is insulin. Among the given options, changes in 29-30 amino acids in the B chain cause the generation of short and long-acting insulins depending on the modification.

Structure:

The primary structure of insulin consists of 2 polypeptide chains: A-chain(21 Amino acids) and B-chain(30 amino acids).

It has two interchain disulfide bonds,

• Between 7th amino acid of A chain and 7th amino acid of B chain
• Between 20th amino acid of A chain and 19th amino acid of B chain

One intrachain disulfide bond is present between the 6th amino acid of A-chain and 11th amino acid in A-chain.

Modification:

Various short and long-acting insulin analogs have been developed by modifying these amino acid residues.

• Insulin lispro: Proline at position 28 and lysine at position 29 in the B-chain are interchanged.
• Insulin Aspart: Proline at position 28 in the B-chain is replaced by aspartic acid.
• Insulin glulisine: Asparagine at position 3 and lysine at position 29 in the B-chain are replaced by lysine and glutamic acid.
• Insulin glargine: Asparagine at position 21 in the A-chain is replaced by glycine and the B-chain contains two extra amino acids(two arginine residues) at positions 31 and 32.
• Insulin detemir: Threonine at position 30 of the B-chain is removed and a 14-carbon fatty acid chain is added to position 29 of the B-chain.
questions.learning: Change in 29-30 in B chain — The hormone shown in the above image is insulin. Among the given options, changes in 29-30 amino acids in the B chain cause the generation of short and long-acting insulins depending on the modification.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is with pentosuria?
questions.explanation: Essential pentosuria is a rare, benign metabolic disorder characterized by the excessive excretion of L-xylulose in the urine. This condition is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme L-xylulose reductase, which normally converts L-xylulose to xylitol in the uronic acid pathway. Patients remain asymptomatic, but the presence of L-xylulose can lead to false-positive results in urine sugar tests for glucose. Regarding the distractors, D-Ribose (Option B) is an essential sugar for nucleotide synthesis and is not typically excreted in this condition. D-Ribulose (Option C) is an intermediate in the pentose phosphate pathway and is similarly not associated with pentosuria. D-Lactose (Option D) is a disaccharide found in milk; its presence in urine (lactosuria) occurs in different clinical contexts, such as late pregnancy or lactation, and is unrelated to pentose metabolism. Thus, L-xylulose is the specific pentose sugar associated with the diagnosis of pentosuria

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a 30-year smoking history presents with an 8-month history of progressive dyspnea and a persistent dry cough. Examination reveals digital clubbing and bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. Pulmonary function tests show FVC at 78% of predicted and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%. Based on these findings and his smoking history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with chronic dyspnea, digital clubbing, and "fine crackles" (Velcro-like rales), which are the hallmark clinical signs of Interstitial Lung Disease. The PFT results show a restrictive pattern: low FVC with a high/normal FEV1/FVC ratio (92%), which rules out obstructive diseases like Asthma (Option A) or COPD (Option D). The provided CT scan provides definitive confirmation, showing a "honeycombing" pattern and traction bronchiectasis. This is the pathognomonic radiological picture of Pulmonary Fibrosis (specifically Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis or UIP). Pulmonary tuberculosis (Option C) would typically show consolidations or cavities rather than diffuse basilar honeycombing. Therefore, the combination of clinical crackles, restrictive lung function, and the classic honeycombing CT appearance makes pulmonary fibrosis the definitive diagnosis. This condition is progressive and irreversible, requiring management of hypoxemia and consideration of antifibrotic therapy
questions.learning: The patient presents with chronic dyspnea, digital clubbing, and "fine crackles" (Velcro-like rales), which are the hallmark clinical signs of Interstitial Lung Disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A lady developed a skin reaction as shown in the image after using a hair dye. Which of the following chemicals is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. p-Phenylenediamine

This is most likely a case of hypersensitivity reaction caused by p-phenylenediamine (PPD), which is present in hair dyes.

Hair dyes such as PPD have the potential to cause contact dermatitis. 10% of PPD users tend to develop contact dermatitis. A patch test is recommended 24-48 hours before its usage either on the forearm or behind the ear. The appearance of any redness, blistering, or swelling implies allergy;  therefore, the application of dye is not recommended. Cross-sensitization with other aromatic benzenes is also noted, which needs to be avoided.

Hair dyes can trigger acute edema and intense pruritus, followed by desquamation. Hair dye can elicit an allergic reaction on the forehead. PPD in the hair dye can also cause an erythema multiforme–like reaction.

In PPD-associated allergies, there is edema and weeping of the scalp margins, eyes, and ears. There may be relative sparing of the scalp. Immediate hypersensitivity reactions present as urticaria, and contact anaphylaxis have also been noted to occur in patients using PPD.  To minimize the risk of an allergic reaction to hair dye, individuals should follow the manufacturer's instructions, perform a patch test, and avoid over-processing the hair. Treatment for PPD-induced contact dermatitis may include topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and in severe cases, oral corticosteroids.

Other options:

Option A: Pollen is not typically found in hair dyes and is not responsible for this condition. Pollen allergies usually present as hay fever or seasonal allergic rhinitis.

Option B: Chromates, which can be found in cement, leather, and paints, are not typically present in hair dyes and are not responsible for this skin reaction.

Option C: Balsam of Peru, a fragrant resin, is found in various cosmetic and food products but is not a common component of hair dyes. It is less likely to be responsible for this condition compared to PPD.
questions.learning: p-Phenylenediamine This is most likely a case of hypersensitivity reaction caused by p-phenylenediamine (PPD), which is present in hair dyes. Hair dyes such as PPD have the potential to cause contact dermatitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

Causes of referred otalgia via the glossopharyngeal nerve include acute pharyngitis, tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, post-tonsillectomy, foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area and an elongated styloid process (Eagle's syndrome).

The ear receives extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

questions.learning: Glossopharyngeal nerve — The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis. The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the finding in the given ultrasound image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phrygian cap

The ultrasound examination of the gallbladder shows a Phrygian cap. It is a normal anatomical variant.

Phrygian cap refers to an anatomical variant of the gallbladder, where, the fundus of the gallbladder folds on itself, or is separated from the body by a partial or complete septum. A true septum is uncommon and is usually an apparent septum due to the gallbladder wall folding. It is an incidental finding that may be seen on CT, MRI, or ultrasound. It causes no symptoms.

The Phrygian cap is named so, due to the resemblance of the ultrasonographic appearance to a hat or cap that is worn by the inhabitants of ancient Phrygia circa 1200 BC.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tooth is the first to erupt in the primary dentition?
questions.explanation: In the normal chronological sequence of dental development, the mandibular (lower) central incisors are the first teeth to erupt into the oral cavity. This typically occurs between the ages of 6 and 10 months. They are followed shortly by the maxillary (upper) central incisors (Option A) at approximately 8 to 12 months. The lateral incisors usually erupt next, followed by the first primary molars. The canines (Options C and D) erupt much later, generally between 16 and 22 months of age. The primary (deciduous) dentition consists of 20 teeth in total. Monitoring the eruption sequence is a key part of pediatric health surveillance, as significant delays or deviations from the normal pattern can indicate systemic conditions, nutritional deficiencies, or localized dental obstructions. Parents often seek guidance during this "teething" phase, which is marked by increased salivation and irritability. Therefore, the lower central incisor marks the functional beginning of the primary dentition
questions.learning: In the normal chronological sequence of dental development, the mandibular (lower) central incisors are the first teeth to erupt into the oral cavity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding accommodative esotropia?
options: It is the most common type of squint.
Miotics are used as the treatment strategy in the high AC/A ratio
It is associated with high myopia.
Refractive type can be fully corrected by use of spectacles.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is associated with high myopia.

Accommodative esotropia is associated with a high degree of hypermetropia (+4 to +7 D).

Accommodative esotropia is the most common type of squint. Typically presents around 2 to 3 years of age.

Types:

1. Refractive

• Associated with high hypermetropia
• Fully correctable by spectacles

2. Non-refractive type

• Abnormal accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio
• Fully corrected by bifocal glasses
• Miotics useful in cases where glasses are unsuitable

• Echothiophate causes iris cyst
• Prevention of iris cysts- Phenylephrine drops

3. Mixed type

The accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio is defined as the amount of convergence measured in prism diopters per unit (diopter) change in accommodation.

The image below shows accommodative esotropia with and without correction.
questions.learning: Accommodative esotropia is associated with a high degree of hypermetropia (+4 to +7 D). Accommodative esotropia is the most common type of squint.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following glucose transporter is present in skeletal muscles and adipose tissues?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GLUT 4

GLUT-4 is present in skeletal muscle cells and adipose tissues.

Glucose transporters, also referred to as GLUTs, are transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitative diffusion. Facilitative diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions through the cell membrane by them binding chemically to a carrier/ transport protein that is responsible for their movement across the cell membrane.

GLUT-4 is a transport protein present in adipocytes. When there is a rise in blood glucose level, insulin secreted by the pancreatic beta cells binds to its receptors on the plasma membrane of adipocytes. Upon binding of insulin to its receptor, activation of the receptor's tyrosine-kinase domain occurs. This activation starts a protein activation cascade leading to the translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane.

Once translocation occurs and GLUT4 is inserted into the plasma membrane, facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient into the cell occurs.

Other options:

Option B: GLUT-2 is found in the liver, pancreatic β cell, small intestine, and kidney. Its function is the rapid uptake or release of glucose.

Option C: GLUT-5 is present in the small intestine and is involved in the absorption of fructose.

Option D: SGLT-1 is a sodium-dependent unidirectional transporter present in the small intestine and kidney that is involved in the active uptake of glucose against a concentration gradient.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the baroreceptors present in the carotid sinus?
options: They need the support of electromechanical transducers
They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer
Afferent fibres pass via cranial nerve IX
They express several non-selective cation channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer

Baroreceptors are not located in the deep smooth muscle layer. They are located in the adventitia layer.

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors which respond to stretch stimuli. They are located in the heart and adventitia of the blood vessels. There are two types of baroreceptors: high-pressure arterial baroreceptors and low-pressure volume receptors. Arterial baroreceptors are located within the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch.

The carotid sinus is a small dilation of the internal carotid artery just above the bifurcation of the common carotid into external and internal carotid branches. The afferent nerve fibres from the carotid sinus form a distinct branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), the carotid sinus nerve.

Afferent signals from both the aortic and carotid sinus baroreceptors are sent to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and they create a negative feedback loop that keeps arterial blood pressure within normal limits.

By stimulating these arterial baroreceptors in response to vascular distension, elevated arterial blood pressure can be reflexively brought back to normal levels by decreasing peripheral sympathetic outflow and activating peripheral parasympathetic outflow.

Three subsequent functional processes must take place in order to convert a mechanical change in the arterial vasculature into an excitatory signal:

1. Vascular distension and the deformation of arterial baroreceptor terminals
2. Mechanoelectrical transduction converts the mechanical deformation of arterial baroreceptor nerve terminals into baroreceptor membrane depolarization. Mechanosensitive ion channels such as the epithelial Na+ channels (ENaCs), acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) and transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels are responsible for mechanoelectrical transduction in arterial baroreceptor nerve terminals.
3. Translation of membrane depolarization into action potentials via voltage-gated ion channels (Na+, Ca2+ and K+).
questions.learning: They are located in the deep smooth muscle layer Baroreceptors are not located in the deep smooth muscle layer. They are located in the adventitia layer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A male was referred to the urology OPD for evaluation of infertility. Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype. Which of the following statements is not true about the condition?
options: Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated.

The clinical features include:

* Eunuchoid body habitus - elongated body and long legs (increased length between the soles and the pubic bone)

* Absence of secondary sexual characteristics - lack of body and facial hair, deep voice

* Small atrophic testes

* Micropenis

* Gynecomastia

* Lower IQ, but no mental retardation

The following hormonal variations are seen in these patients:

* Elevated FSH

* Elevated estradiol

* Low testosterone

* Insulin resistance - increased incidence of type 2 diabetes

Patients with Klinefelter syndrome are at a higher risk for:

* Male breast cancer (20x more common than in normal males)

* Extragonadal germ cell tumors

* Autoimmune diseases - systemic lupus erythematosus
questions.learning: Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Re-infection with which of the following will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

Re-infection with Dengue virus will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies.

The DENV-1/DENV-2 sequence of infection has a 500-fold risk of DHF than primary infection.

DENV-3/DENV-2 sequence has a 150-fold risk and DENV-4/DENV-2 has a 50-fold risk of DHF.

This shows that multiple infection with different serotypes of the dengue virus leads to severe forms of dengue such as DHF/DSS.

Recent update: Dengvaxia is the WHO endorsed first ever vaccine for dengue fever, which is currently licensed in twenty countries.

Other options: Re-infection with Yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and Zika will not cause catastrophic symptoms in the presence of antibodies.
questions.learning: Dengue Re-infection with Dengue virus will lead to catastrophic symptoms even in the presence of antibodies. The DENV-1/DENV-2 sequence of infection has a 500-fold risk of DHF than primary infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a mobile, warm to touch nodule in the neck. On the anaerobic culture of the biopsy material from this swelling, it showed colonies as shown in the image which had gram-positive branching rods on staining. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Penicillin

The given image shows molar tooth colonies that are characteristic of Actinomyces species. The given clinical scenario of a mobile, warm to touch nodule in the neck describes cervicofacial actinomycosis also known as 'lumpy jaw syndrome'. Penicillin is the drug of choice for actinomyces infection.

Actinomyces are Gram-positive anaerobic bacilli that produce molar tooth colonies on incubation for 72 hours on brain-heart infusion agar. They cause a chronic suppurative and granulomatous infection called actinomycosis. It can present as one of the following clinical types:

• Cervicofacial type- Fluctuant mass in the jaw area producing draining fistulas.
• Thoracic type- Pulmonary infection with fever, cough, and purulent sputum.
• Abdominal type- Occurs following ruptured appendix or ulcer. It may spread throughout the peritoneum and involve multiple organs.

Actinomycosis can spread to bones and surrounding tissue and produce multiple discharging sinuses. Treatment requires prolonged administration of penicillin for 6–12 months. In penicillin-allergic patients, clindamycin or erythromycin is effective. Surgical excision and drainage may be required in some cases.

The given image shows cervicofacial actinomycosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In which of the following reflexes, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enterogastric

In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum.

When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which passes back to the stomach. These reflexes slow or stop the stomach emptying if the volume of the chyme in the duodenum becomes too much. These reflexes are called enterogastric reflexes.

This reflex can be triggered due to the following reasons:

• Presence of irritants and acids in duodenal chyme (most sensitive factor)
• Distension of duodenum due to the presence of an excessive volume of chyme
• Rapid entry of hypertonic or hypotonic fluids into the duodenum
• Presence of breakdown products of protein digestion and sometimes fat
questions.learning: Enterogastric — In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum. When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which passes back to the stomach.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following contributes to the latent period in a single muscle twitch? a. Excitation-contraction coupling b. Opening of sodium channels on NMJ c. Transmission of impulse from the site of stimulus to NMJ d. Pumping of calcium back to the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a, b, c

The latent period of a muscle twitch is the short delay (≈2–5 ms) between stimulus application and start of contraction.

This period includes all events before actual cross-bridge cycling begins. The latent period represents the time between stimulus and onset of contraction and includes electrical and coupling events before tension develops. It covers impulse transmission to the NMJ, opening of Na⁺ channels with depolarization, and excitation–contraction coupling with Ca²⁺ release. Pumping Ca²⁺ back into the SR occurs during relaxation, not latency. Hence a, b, and c contribute to the latent period.

Stimulus applied

↓

Impulse travels along motor nerve (c)

↓

Acetylcholine release at NMJ → Na⁺ channels open (b)

↓

End plate potential → Muscle action potential

↓

T-tubule depolarization

↓

Ca²⁺ release from SR (Excitation-Contraction Coupling) (a)

↓

Actin-myosin interaction begins → Contraction starts

Latent period reflects 3 physiological delays:

1. Neural delay

• Nerve conduction time

2. Synaptic delay (\~0.5 ms)

• ACh release, diffusion, receptor binding

3. E-C coupling delay

• T-tubule depolarization
• DHPR–RyR interaction
• Ca²⁺ release

Most important contributor: Excitation–contraction coupling
questions.learning: a, b, c The latent period of a muscle twitch is the short delay (≈2–5 ms) between stimulus application and start of contraction. This period includes all events before actual cross-bridge cycling begins.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman complaints of inability to conceive, dysmenorrhea, and pelvic pain. She has a history of frequent pelvic inflammatory disease. Hysterosalpingogram shows an absence of peritoneal spillage on the right side. Identify the given clinical scenario.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tubal block

The given clinical scenario is indicative of a tubal block.

The presenting complaints of tubal block are:

* Dysmenorrhea

* Pelvic pain

* Inability to conceive

* Repeated episodes of PID

* History of ectopic pregnancy

Tubal block can be due to:

* Strictures - fibrotic block

* Inspissated amorphous material

* Tubal spasm - This can occur in apprehensive patients. It is prevented by premedication with atropine and analgesia

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a technique used for visualization of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes by the injection of a radio-opaque dye, and visualization of the dye by fluoroscopy as it passes through the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes. It is best performed between the end of the menstrual period and ovulation (i.e 9th or 10th day of the cycle). 10-15ml of the dye is injected using a Leech-Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter. If the tubes are patent, the dye will spill out of the tubal Ostia and smear the adjacent bowel.
questions.learning: Tubal block — The given clinical scenario is indicative of a tubal block. The presenting complaints of tubal block are: * Dysmenorrhea * Pelvic pain * Inability to conceive * Repeated episodes of PID * History of ectopic pregnancy Tubal block can be due…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Urinary tract infection in a pregnant lady in her 2nd trimester is best defined as:
options: Growth of 10^3 coliform in suprapubic sample
Growth of 10^5 coliform in voided urine sample
Frequency with dysuria with positive nitrite and leucoesterase dipstick test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Growth of 10^5 coliform in voided urine sample

Urinary tract infection (UTI) in a pregnant lady in her 2nd trimester is best defined as the growth of 105 coliforms in a voided urine sample. Urine culture is the standard method to evaluate UTI pregnancy.

UTI in pregnancy is a bacterial infection caused by organisms in the normal perineal flora. It can vary from asymptomatic bacteriuria to symptomatic cystitis or pyelonephritis.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is characterized by persistent and actively multiplying bacteria in the urinary tract without any symptoms. A positive culture is demonstrated during the antenatal visit. It can complicate into a symptomatic infection when untreated.

Symptomatic infections include

• Cystitis is characterized by dysuria, urgency and frequency along with pyuria and bacteriuria. Microscopic hematuria is also seen
• Pyelonephritis is common in the second trimester, nulliparous and young women. It is usually unilateral with fever, chills, and ache in the lumbar region. Nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral tenderness may be seen. The organisms causing pyelonephritis are E. coli >> Streptococcus, S.aureus > Enterobacter, Klebsiella

UTI is evaluated by blood studies including complete blood count, serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, urine studies and imaging. Urine studies mainly include a urine culture, urine analysis, and dipstick.

Urine culture is the standard method of evaluating UTIs in pregnancy. Positive urine culture shows a bacterial growth of >100,000 colony-forming units (CFUs) per milliliter in a voided urine sample. The presence of white blood cell (WBC) casts is suggestive of pyelonephritis. No other screening methods are as reliable as a urine culture.

Urine analysis showing positive nitrites, leukocyte esterase, WBCs (pyuria), red blood cells (RBCs), and protein are suggestive of UTI. Pyuria is seen in cystitis. Dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase is used to evaluate asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Management of UTIs is as follows

• Asymptomatic bacteriuria is mainly treated with oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin, ampicillin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
• Pyelonephritis is managed with intravenous hydration, and antibiotics such as ampicillin+gentamycin, cefazolin or ceftriaxone.
questions.learning: Growth of 10^5 coliform in voided urine sample Urinary tract infection (UTI) in a pregnant lady in her 2nd trimester is best defined as the growth of 105 coliforms in a voided urine sample.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and diarrhea. On further evaluation, the patient was found to have cutaneous flushing, extensive wheeze, and tricuspid insufficiency. Contrast enhanced-MRI revealed the presence of endocardial fibrosis. Which of the following substances will be excreted excessively in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-Hydroxy indole acetic acid

5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) will be excreted excessively in the above given clinical scenario, as this is a case of carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA. It is characterized by cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea.

Note:

5-HIAA testing is a 24-hour urine test that is specific to carcinoid tumours. This test is the most common biochemical test for carcinoid tumours associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Pearl PF0663: Carcinoid syndrome
questions.learning: 5-Hydroxy indole acetic acid 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) will be excreted excessively in the above given clinical scenario, as this is a case of carcinoid syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling, and biopsy of the lesion reveals characteristic “Orphan Annie eye” nuclei. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
questions.explanation: In thyroid pathology, the presence of "Orphan Annie’s eye" nuclei is pathognomonic for Papillary Carcinoma, the most common type of thyroid cancer. These nuclei are characteristically large and appear "optically clear" or empty with peripheral chromatin condensation, resembling the eyes of the comic strip character. Other classic histological features of papillary carcinoma include "Psammoma bodies" (laminated calcifications) and nuclear grooves. Follicular carcinoma (Option A) is characterized by a thick capsule and vascular/capsular invasion without these specific nuclear changes. Medullary carcinoma (Option D) arises from C-cells and shows amyloid stroma on histology. Toxic nodular goiter (Option C) is a benign condition resulting in hyperthyroidism. Papillary carcinoma typically has an excellent prognosis and tends to spread via the lymphatics to cervical lymph nodes. Identifying these specific nuclear "ground-glass" appearances on Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) or biopsy is a fundamental skill for diagnosing midline neck masses

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which structure involvement is responsible for the clinical presentation depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts significant, non-pitting, asymmetrical edema of the left foot, which is characteristic of lymphedema. In the majority of cases, lymphedema is caused by the dysfunction or obstruction of the superficial lymphatic system. The superficial lymphatics drain the skin and subcutaneous tissues and are responsible for the vast majority of lymphatic drainage from the limbs. When these vessels are damaged (by infection like filariasis, trauma, or surgery), protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitial space, leading to the firm swelling seen here. Deep lymphatics (Option B) primarily drain muscles and joints and are less commonly the primary site of clinical lymphedema presentation. Superficial vein involvement (Option C) would typically present as varicose veins or pitting edema associated with venous insufficiency. Primary skin conditions (Option D) do not cause this type of structural swelling. Therefore, the clinical presentation of chronic, localized limb swelling is most directly linked to an impairment in the superficial lymphatic drainage

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: New A patient with leprosy presented with the deformity as shown below. Which nerve injury causes the given condition ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given image shows extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joints of the ring and little finger, caused by ulnar nerve injury. It produces a claw hand (main en griffe). Leprosy can affect peripheral nerves and lead to their associated conditions.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals in the hand. The lumbricals have a combined action on metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint flexion and interphalangeal (IP) joint extension (glass holding posture). In ulnar nerve injury, since the medial lumbricals are not functional, the forearm muscles are unopposed. Hence, there is hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints. This causes claw hand deformity. There is also numbness of the ulnar one and a half fingers.

Elbow fractures or dislocations lead to high lesions of the ulnar nerve. Here, the hand is not markedly deformed because the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed and the fingers, therefore, appear less clawed. This is called the high ulnar paradox.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book forcefully while the doctor tries to pull it. In a positive test, due to weakness of adductor pollicis muscle, adduction of thumb is lost. The patient tries to hold the book by using flexor pollicis longus muscle. This produces flexion at the inter-phalangeal joint while holding the book.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, it is easy for the examiner to pull out the card when held between the fingers. This is due to the loss of adduction by palmar interossei muscles.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to 'ape thumb' deformity. In forearm or elbow injuries, there is paralysis of long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, radial wrist flexors, and forearm pronators. This leads to the characteristic 'pointing index finger'. There is sensory loss over three and a half digits on the radial side.

Option D -Posterior interosseous nerve injury, is seen in posterior interosseous syndrome. The wrist is in radial deviation and there is loss of metacarpophalangeal joint extension. However, wrist extension is preserved.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Melanosis coli (brownish discoloration of colonic mucosa) can occur due to the long-term consumption of which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stimulant laxatives

Melanosis coli is a benign brown-black pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria. It is classically associated with long-term use of anthraquinone-containing stimulant laxatives, such as senna and cascara.

Why not the other options?

• B. NSAIDs: Can cause gastritis, peptic ulceration, and enteropathy, but are not a classic cause of melanosis coli.
• C. Proton pump inhibitors: Not associated with melanosis coli.
• D. 3rd-generation cephalosporins: May cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea/C. difficile infection but do not cause melanosis coli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 75-year-old man presented with temporal headache, jaw pain, exacerbated by chewing and talking. Which one of the following investigations will most likely help in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal artery biopsy

Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically affecting individuals >50 years of age. It presents with new-onset temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms. Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and should be performed promptly, although high-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately if the diagnosis is suspected to prevent irreversible blindness.

• A. Temporal artery biopsy:

• Gold standard investigation for Giant Cell Arteritis.
• Shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, disruption of the internal elastic lamina, and intimal thickening.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Electromyography: Used to evaluate neuromuscular disorders, not vasculitis.
• C. MRI of the brain: May exclude intracranial pathology but does not diagnose Giant Cell Arteritis.
• D. Carotid colour Doppler: Evaluates carotid artery disease and stroke risk, but is not the diagnostic test for temporal arteritis.
questions.learning: Temporal artery biopsy Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically affecting individuals >50 years of age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: This instrument is contraindicated for?
questions.explanation: Obstetric forceps are instruments designed to assist in the vaginal delivery of the fetal head by providing traction or rotation. Their use is strictly contraindicated in cases of obstructed labor. In obstructed labor, there is a physical mismatch (such as cephalopelvic disproportion) that prevents safe passage; applying forceps in this situation can lead to catastrophic maternal and fetal injuries, including uterine rupture and fetal skull fractures. Regarding the other options, forceps can be used during a Caesarean section (Option A) to help extract a deeply engaged head. Specific types, like Piper forceps, are used for the after-coming head of a breech (Option C). Kielland forceps are used for rotation in occipital posterior positions (Option D). Therefore, only obstructed labor presents a complete contraindication to their use, necessitating an immediate surgical alternative like a C-section
questions.learning: Obstetric forceps are instruments designed to assist in the vaginal delivery of the fetal head by providing traction or rotation. Their use is strictly contraindicated in cases of obstructed labor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with chest pain and hoarseness for one month, and on a CT angiogram, the following image is seen, what is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Saccular aneurysm of distal aorta

The given CT shows saccular aneurysm of the distal aorta. The clinical presentation of chest pain and hoarseness supports the diagnosis.

Other options:

Option A: Stenosis of the aortic arch would show a narrowing rather than an aneurysmal dilation, and it is more likely to present with symptoms related to decreased blood flow to the upper body.

Option B: Aortic dissection would usually present with a tearing chest pain that radiates to the back and would show a double lumen or false lumen on imaging. The below image shows Stanford type A aortic dissection:

Option D: Coarctation of the aorta typically presents with hypertension in the upper limbs and weak or absent pulses in the lower limbs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension. He has a history of renal stones and has experienced a few episodes of renal colic. Which diuretic is the most appropriate to use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrochlorothiazide

Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption. This helps prevent recurrent calcium renal stones while effectively treating hypertension.

Thiazide

↓

↓ NaCl reabsorption (DCT)

↓

↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger)

↓

↓ Urinary Ca²⁺ (hypocalciuria)

↓

↓ Calcium stone formation

Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, and spironolactone has no role in stone prevention.

| Diuretic | Site | Effect on Ca²⁺ | Stone Risk

| -------- | ---- | -------------- | ----------

| Thiazide | DCT | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺ | ✅ Prevents stones

| Loop (Furosemide) | TAL | ↑ urinary Ca²⁺ | ❌ Promotes stones

| K⁺-sparing | Collecting duct | Neutral | No effect

| Problem | Drug Benefit

| ------- | ------------

| Hypertension | Thiazide lowers BP

| Recurrent Ca stones | ↓ urinary Ca²⁺
questions.learning: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide reduces urinary calcium excretion by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption. This helps prevent recurrent calcium renal stones while effectively treating hypertension.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a sudden onset of severe sore throat and breathing difficulty that began a few hours earlier. His condition has rapidly worsened, and he is now sitting upright in a tripod position, drooling excessively, appearing anxious, and speaking in a muffled voice. He has a high-grade fever (103.1°F) and noisy breathing with inspiratory stridor on examination. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: The child presents with sudden onset high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, inspiratory stridor, muffled voice, and tripod position, which are classic features of acute epiglottitis, a life-threatening upper airway obstruction. The condition progresses rapidly and requires urgent airway management. The most common causative organism of epiglottitis is Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), a bacterium. However, since this option is not provided, the closest correct answer among the given options is Influenza virus, which can cause severe upper respiratory tract infections and may be associated with similar clinical presentations or secondary bacterial infection. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) → Causes bronchiolitis, mainly affecting lower airways (C) Parainfluenza virus → Causes croup, which presents with barking cough and gradual onset (D) Newcastle disease virus → Primarily affects birds, not humans
questions.learning: The child presents with sudden onset high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, inspiratory stridor, muffled voice, and tripod position, which are classic features of acute epiglottitis, a life-threatening upper airway obstruction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with vision loss. On radiological investigation, an aneurysm causing damage to the optic chiasma was noted. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the artery that is causing the damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior communicating artery

An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

Circle of Willis is a large arterial anastomosis that unites the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. It lies in the subarachnoid space within the basal cisterns that surround the optic chiasma and infundibulum.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm:

Anterior communicating artery (Acom) links the right and left anterior cerebral arteries and is directed anterior and superior to the optic chiasma. The aneurysm will protrude in the posterior direction and will impinge upon the optic chiasma from above, leading to loss of vision.

Compression of the optic chiasma (central lesion) by an ACom aneurysm, will lead to bitemporal hemianopia i.e, loss of vision in the left/temporal halves of both visual fields. Nasal fibers of each retina cross through the chiasma at this level and hence, these fibers will be compromised.

In the case of a bilateral peripheral lesion of the optic chiasma, binasal hemianopia will be seen.

Other causes of chiasmal lesions are

• Pituitary adenoma (most common)
• Craniopharyngioma
• Meningioma
• Glioma

Blood supply of optic chiasma: The left and right anterior cerebral arteries, along with the superior hypophyseal artery (branch of the internal carotid artery) form the blood supply of optic chiasma.

The given cadaveric image below is of the vascular structures (Circle of Willis) at the base of the brain.

Investigation: Digital subtraction angiogram is the definitive imaging modality for aneurysms arising from the circle of Willis. Other investigations are CT and MRI.

Other options:

Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery (option B) and middle cerebral artery (option C) aneurysms will not compress the optic chiasma as they are anatomically not in close proximity to be able to exert pressure on the chiasma and cause loss of vision.

Despite the anatomical proximity of the anterior cerebral artery (option D) to the optic chiasma, anterior communicating artery (Acom) aneurysm is the commonest intracranial aneurysm.
questions.learning: Anterior communicating artery — An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor receives two separate court summons on the same day: one to appear as a witness in a murder trial, and another to provide an expert opinion in a case of medical negligence involving wrong leg amputation. According to legal priority, which case should the doctor attend first?
options: Appearance for providing opinion on negligence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Appearance for murder case

When a doctor receives multiple court summons on the same day, priority is given to criminal cases involving serious offences (e.g., murder) over civil or expert opinion cases.

• Hierarchy of legal priority:

• Criminal cases (especially grave offences like murder) take precedence
• Over civil cases or expert testimony (e.g., medical negligence)

• Reason:

• Criminal cases involve state prosecution and serious offences against society

Doctor’s responsibility:

• Attend the higher-priority court (murder case)
• Inform the other court in advance and request adjournment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following drugs decreases the serum parathyroid hormone levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcitriol

Correct answer is B because calcitriol (active vitamin D) increases intestinal calcium absorption and raises serum calcium, which suppresses parathyroid hormone via negative feedback.

Key regulators of PTH:

| Factor | Effect on PTH

| ------ | -------------

| Low Ca²⁺ | ↑ PTH

| High Ca²⁺ | ↓ PTH

| Calcitriol | ↓ PTH

| Phosphate | ↑ PTH

Calcitriol acts on:

| Organ | Effect

| ----- | ------

| Intestine | ↑ Ca absorption

| Kidney | ↑ Ca reabsorption

| Bone | ↑ remodeling

Risedronate reduces bone resorption but does not directly suppress PTH. Lithium can increase PTH and cause hyperparathyroidism. Diuretics have variable effects and are not primary PTH suppressors.
questions.learning: Calcitriol Correct answer is B because calcitriol (active vitamin D) increases intestinal calcium absorption and raises serum calcium, which suppresses parathyroid hormone via negative feedback.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Prolonged exposure to high partial pressure of oxygen causes pulmonary capillary endothelial damage, leading to alveolar inflammation and edema. This phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lorrain–Smith effect

Lorrain–Smith effect refers to pulmonary oxygen toxicity caused by prolonged exposure to high partial pressures of oxygen (hyperoxia).

• Excess oxygen leads to formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
• ROS cause damage to pulmonary capillary endothelium and alveolar epithelium.
• This results in alveolar inflammation, pulmonary edema, and decreased lung compliance.

Clinical settings:

• Prolonged oxygen therapy
• Hyperbaric oxygen exposure
• Diving or high-pressure environments

Other effects:

A. Paul Bert effect: CNS oxygen toxicity → seizures due to high oxygen pressure.

C. Bohr effect: Effect of CO₂ and pH on hemoglobin oxygen affinity.

D. Haldane effect: Oxygenation of hemoglobin reduces CO₂ carrying capacity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the type of myoma labeled as '4' in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pedunculated submucosal myoma

The type of myoma labeled as '4' is pedunculated submucosal myoma.

Uterine myomas are broadly classified into 3 types.

They are:

* Intramural: remains within the myometrial wall.

* Submucous: present inside the uterine cavity and covered only by a thin endometrium.

* Subserous: present towards the peritoneal surface.

Treatment includes:

* Hormones to shrink the fibroid

* Uterine artery embolization.

* Myomectomy.

* Total / subtotal hysterectomy.
